NAMES.name: faraday_angle
NAMES.short:
Faraday rotation of a probing wave’s polarization plane caused by electron
density and the magnetic-field component along its plasma path.
NAMES.long:
The Faraday angle is the signed rotation of a probing electromagnetic wave’s
polarization plane caused by propagation through magnetized plasma. For an
equilibrium state, it is the angle predicted from the electron density and
magnetic field encountered along the beam path.

In the cold, weakly dispersive magnetoionic approximation, the
plasma-induced rotation is defined by

$$
\theta_F = \frac{e^3\lambda^2}{8\pi^2\epsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(\ell) B_{\parallel}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\theta_F$ is the Faraday rotation angle, $e$ is the elementary-charge
magnitude, $\lambda$ is the probing-wave vacuum wavelength, $\pi$ is the
circle constant, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ is the
electron mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $\mathcal{L}$ is the segment of
the beam path crossing the plasma, $\ell$ is distance along that path,
$n_e(\ell)$ is the local electron number density, and $B_{\parallel}(\ell)$
is the signed magnetic-field component along the beam direction.

The quantity applies to the electron contribution accumulated along one
probing beam through the plasma. Its aggregation is a line integral along
that path, not a local rotation rate, flux-surface average, or sum over
multiple beams; optical rotation produced outside the plasma is excluded.
The equilibrium-derived value is the rotation predicted by the reconstructed
plasma state and is distinct from a directly observed angle or from a
residual between prediction and observation.

Faraday angle describes rotation of the polarization plane, whereas
[polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter
beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the
signed shape of the polarization ellipse through its axis ratio; the two
quantities are not interchangeable.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the polarization plane rotates according to
the right-hand rule about the beam propagation direction from its incident
reference orientation.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of reciprocal major radius, providing a geometric
equilibrium coefficient for toroidal geometry in flux-coordinate equations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric average of the reciprocal major radius over a
complete magnetic flux surface. It is an equilibrium metric coefficient
independent of plasma species, population, magnetic-field component, and
physical transport process.

For a magnetic flux surface identified by the label $\psi$, the defining
flux-surface average is:

$$
g_{1/R}(\psi) =
\left\langle \frac{1}{R} \right\rangle_\psi =
\frac{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{S}(\psi)}
\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}\,\frac{1}{R}}
{\displaystyle\oint_{\mathcal{S}(\psi)}
\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
$$

Here $g_{1/R}$ denotes the metric coefficient, $R$ is the major-radius
coordinate, $\psi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $\mathcal{S}(\psi)$
is the corresponding closed magnetic flux surface, $dS$ is its surface-area
element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux-surface label.
The coordinate $R$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle and $Z$ is the vertical
coordinate.

The aggregation is over the entire closed flux surface using the
flux-surface weighting shown in the defining relation; this is not the local
reciprocal radius at a point. The quantity is distinct from the flux-surface
average of reciprocal squared major radius, [flux-surface-averaged inverse
square of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius).

It is the flux-surface-averaged specialization of [inverse major
radius](name:inverse_of_major_radius): the averaging operator is applied to
the local reciprocal-major-radius quantity without introducing a species,
field-component, or process restriction.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of total magnetic-field
strength, a geometric coefficient in neoclassical and flux-surface-averaged
transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the
total magnetic-field strength on a nested magnetic surface. It captures
field-strength geometry independently of the magnetic-field direction.

The defining relation is

$$
\left\langle \frac{1}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_\psi
=
\frac{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} |\mathbf{B}|^{-2}\,\frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
{\displaystyle \int_{S(\psi)} \frac{dS}{|\nabla\psi|}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its
magnitude, $\psi$ is the flux-surface label, $S(\psi)$ is the magnetic
surface labeled by $\psi$, $dS$ is its surface-area element, and
$\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux-surface label.

The quantity applies to the complete magnetic flux surface and uses the
inverse-$|\nabla\psi|$ weighting shown in the defining relation. It is not a
pointwise inverse-square field value and has no selection by magnetic-field
direction, component, species, or source.

It is the flux-surface-averaged transformation of the parent [inverse square
of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), with the
reciprocal square formed locally before averaging. It is distinct from
[flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude) and
[flux-surface-averaged square of magnetic-field
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
because nonlinear inversion and squaring do not commute with surface
averaging.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of reciprocal squared major radius, providing a
geometric metric coefficient for parallel-gradient and neoclassical
transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the
major radius on a nested equilibrium magnetic flux surface. It is a positive
geometric metric coefficient used in parallel-gradient operators and
neoclassical and gyrokinetic transport equations.

It is defined by

$$
g_{m1}(\psi)=\left\langle \frac{1}{R^2}\right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $g_{m1}$ denotes this metric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius
measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic
flux labeling the surface, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes the
flux-surface average on that surface.

The quantity applies to the entire magnetic flux surface and has no species,
field-component, or source-process restriction. Its aggregation convention
is a flux-surface average of the local reciprocal-square geometric factor;
it is not the reciprocal square of a flux-surface-averaged major radius.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the pointwise [inverse of square of
major radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius). It differs from the
related [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages
the first reciprocal power of $R$ rather than its reciprocal square.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to points on a nested magnetic flux surface, giving the mean
major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this
flux-surface-averaged quantity, that distance is averaged over each nested
magnetic flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

The flux-surface average of major radius is defined by

$$
\langle R\rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi R\,dl/B_p}{\oint_\psi dl/B_p}
$$

where $\langle R\rangle_\psi$ is the averaged major-radius coordinate,
$\psi$ is the magnetic-flux label identifying the surface, $l$ is poloidal
arc length along that surface, and $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal
magnetic field. The contour integral extends around the complete poloidal
intersection of the nested magnetic flux surface.

This quantity applies to a complete magnetic flux surface and aggregates the
local [major radius] using the flux-surface weighting defined by the inverse
poloidal-field magnitude. It is therefore distinct from pointwise major
radius and contains no point-specific or localized evaluation.

The quantity is the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [major radius]. It
must not be confused with [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages
the reciprocal $1/R$ rather than averaging $R$ itself; consequently, it is
not generally the reciprocal of that neighboring average.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_parallel_current_density
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is the signed scalar defined
on each magnetic flux surface as the flux-surface average of the plasma
current-density vector dotted with the magnetic-field vector, divided by a
single global reference field B0.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density is the scalar current-density
quantity defined on a magnetic flux surface by averaging the scalar product
of the plasma current-density vector with the magnetic-field vector and
normalizing by a single global reference magnetic-field scalar. It describes
the current density parallel to the magnetic field only through this
flux-surface-averaged, reference-field-normalized definition.

For a magnetic flux surface $S$, the defining relationship is

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{fs}}(S) = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_S}{B_0}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{fs}}(S)$ is the flux-surface-averaged parallel
current density on $S$, $\mathbf{j}$ is the [plasma current-density
vector](name:current_density), $\mathbf{B}$ is the [magnetic-field
vector](name:magnetic_field), $\left\langle \cdot \right\rangle_S$ denotes
the flux-surface average over $S$, and $B_0$ is a single global reference
magnetic-field scalar.

The scope is magnetic flux surfaces in the plasma for which a flux-surface
average is defined. The aggregation convention is to average
$\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ over each surface first and then divide by the
same $B_0$ for every surface; $B_0$ is not a function of the flux-surface
label.

This quantity is not the local [parallel current
density](name:parallel_current_density) and is not the flux-surface average
of that local component, because the definition normalizes by $B_0$ rather
than by the local magnetic-field magnitude. Multiplying this quantity by
$B_0$ gives the flux-surface average $\left\langle
\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_S$.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\left\langle
\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle_S$ has the same sign as the global
reference magnetic field $B_0$.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude divided by the squared local magnetic-field magnitude, a metric
coefficient for equilibrium geometry.
NAMES.long:
This coefficient describes the flux-surface-averaged geometric weighting of
a toroidal-flux radial coordinate by the inverse square of the local
magnetic-field magnitude.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}_B = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}_B$ is the averaged metric coefficient,
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla$ is
the spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes the average over a magnetic flux
surface.

The quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces and uses
the average of the pointwise ratio, not the ratio of separately averaged
numerator and denominator. It is nonnegative because both the gradient
magnitude and magnetic-field magnitude are squared.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the local [ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared magnetic-field
magnitude](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude).
It shares the gradient-squared geometric factor with the
[flux-surface-averaged squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
but additionally applies the pointwise inverse-square magnetic-field
weighting before averaging. It is distinct from the corresponding
major-radius denominator variant, [flux-surface-averaged ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface-averaged magnetic-geometry coefficient measuring the squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient relative to the squared major radius.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a magnetic-geometry metric coefficient that characterizes
how a toroidal-flux radial coordinate varies across nested magnetic
surfaces, with the variation weighted by inverse squared major radius.

It is defined by

$$
g_2 = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho|^2}{R^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $g_2$ is the flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient, $\rho$ is the
toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla\rho$ is its spatial gradient,
$|\nabla\rho|$ is the gradient magnitude, $R$ is the major radius, and the
subscript $\mathrm{FS}$ denotes the prescribed average over a complete
magnetic flux surface.

The quantity applies to an equilibrium magnetic flux surface and represents
an aggregate over that surface rather than a pointwise local value. It has
no species, population, or transport-channel restriction.

It is the flux-surface average of the local ratio defined by [ratio of
square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient magnitude to square of major
radius](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).
Unlike [flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
it retains the inverse-square-major-radius weighting; the numerator is
constructed from the [toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the total equilibrium
magnetic field, providing a geometric coefficient for equilibrium and
neoclassical transport relations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the surface-averaged squared strength of the total magnetic
field on a nested magnetic flux surface. It is a geometric metric
coefficient used in equilibrium descriptions and in bounce-averaged and
neoclassical transport relations.

The flux-surface average is defined by

$$
\left\langle B^2 \right\rangle_\psi = \frac{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{B^2}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)} \frac{1}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}\,dS}
$$

where $B^2$ is the [square of the magnetic-field
magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), $\psi$ is the poloidal
magnetic-flux label of the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the closed magnetic flux
surface with that label, $\nabla\psi$ is the gradient of the flux label, and
$dS$ is the surface-area element.

The quantity applies to the total equilibrium magnetic field, including all
of its components, and is aggregated over each closed flux surface with the
inverse-$\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert$ weighting shown above. It is not the
pointwise value of $B^2$, the square of a flux-surface-averaged
magnetic-field magnitude, or a single magnetic-field component.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of
[square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude).
It differs from
[flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages the field magnitude before squaring, and from
[flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude),
which averages its reciprocal.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the
normalized toroidal-flux radius. It is the averaged contravariant radial
metric coefficient for the flux coordinate rho_tor.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the gradient of the
toroidal flux coordinate is the average, over one magnetic flux surface, of
the squared norm of $\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}$. It is the
flux-surface-averaged contravariant radial metric coefficient associated
with the radial coordinate in the flux-coordinate system
$(\rho_\mathrm{tor}, \theta, \phi)$, where $\theta$ is a poloidal angle
label and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity is defined by the flux-surface average of the local radial
metric component:

$$
G_{\rho\rho}(\rho_\mathrm{tor}) = \left\langle |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2 \right\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}} = \frac{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2\, dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}{\int_{S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})} dA / |\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|}
$$

where $G_{\rho\rho}$ denotes this flux-surface-averaged metric coefficient,
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux radius,
$S(\rho_\mathrm{tor})$ is the magnetic flux surface with that label,
$\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, $dA$ is the surface-area element,
and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}$ denotes averaging over that
flux surface.

The coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is constituted by
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}=\sqrt{\Phi/\Phi_b}$, where $\Phi$ is the toroidal
magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface and $\Phi_b$ is its value at the
plasma boundary. The scope is closed nested equilibrium flux surfaces; the
aggregation convention is an average over the entire surface at fixed
$\rho_\mathrm{tor}$.

This is not the pointwise quantity $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|^2$, not the
flux-surface average of $|\nabla \rho_\mathrm{tor}|$, and not a volume or
time average. It belongs to the same flux-surface-averaged geometric-metric
family as the [flux-surface-averaged inverse major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), but it
characterizes the radial metric of the normalized toroidal-flux radius
rather than a major-radius factor.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_current_density
NAMES.short:
Geometry-weighted flux-surface average of the net conventional toroidal
current density driving the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux distribution.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the effective net conventional current density associated
with the toroidal direction on each closed magnetic flux surface. It
represents the toroidal current source entering the equilibrium relation for
the poloidal magnetic-flux distribution.

It is defined by

$$
J_{\phi}^{\mathrm{FS}} = \frac{\left\langle j_{\mathrm{tor}}/R \right\rangle}{\left\langle 1/R \right\rangle}
$$

where $J_{\phi}^{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged toroidal current
density, $j_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the local conventional current-density
component in the toroidal direction, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes a magnetic flux-surface average. The toroidal
direction is the increasing-$\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is vertical.

The quantity applies to the net current carried by all included
charged-particle populations on a closed magnetic flux surface. The
weighting by $1/R$ is part of the definition; this is not an unweighted
arithmetic average of $j_{\mathrm{tor}}$. It is distinct from
toroidal_current_density, which denotes the local toroidal component, and
from [toroidal_total_current_density](name:toroidal_total_current_density),
which denotes a total toroidal current-density quantity without this
flux-surface-averaging transformation. Its flux-surface integral
relationship to the net plasma current is represented by
[plasma_current](name:plasma_current).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the net conventional toroidal current density
on the flux surface points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Flux surface averaged toroidal current density = average(j_tor/R) / average(1/R)

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Geometric metric coefficient formed by averaging the local magnitude of the
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient over each nested magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average of the local geometric rate at
which the toroidal flux coordinate changes through physical space. It is a
scalar metric coefficient associated with nested magnetic surfaces.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}) = \left\langle \left|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}\right| \right\rangle_{\mathcal{S}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S})$ is the averaged metric coefficient,
$\mathcal{S}$ is a magnetic flux surface, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the
toroidal flux coordinate labeling nested magnetic surfaces, $\nabla$ is the
spatial gradient, and the angle brackets with subscript $\mathcal{S}$ denote
averaging over that surface.

The quantity applies to the complete nested magnetic flux surface and is
aggregated over the surface rather than evaluated at a point, along a line,
or over a volume. It represents the average of the gradient magnitude, not a
directional component and not the local unaveraged value.

It is obtained by applying flux-surface averaging to the local [toroidal
flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude). Unlike
[flux-surface-averaged square of toroidal flux coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
it averages the magnitude itself rather than its square.

NAMES.name: gap_at_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short:
Minimum geometric clearance between the plasma separatrix and the nearest
limiter or wall element, evaluated at the closest-wall point.
NAMES.long:
The gap is the shortest geometric separation between the plasma separatrix,
or last closed flux surface, and the nearest wall or limiter element. It
quantifies the boundary clearance at the wall location where this separation
is smallest.

$$
g_{\mathrm{cw}} = \min_{\mathbf{x}_s \in \mathcal{S},\,\mathbf{x}_w \in \mathcal{W} \cup \mathcal{L}} \left\|\mathbf{x}_s - \mathbf{x}_w\right\|
$$

Here, $g_{\mathrm{cw}}$ is the closest-wall gap, $\mathcal{S}$ is the plasma
separatrix, $\mathcal{W}$ is the wall surface, $\mathcal{L}$ is the limiter
surface, $\mathbf{x}_s$ and $\mathbf{x}_w$ are points on those surfaces, and
$\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean distance.

The quantity is an aggregate minimum over the full separatrix and all
relevant wall or limiter elements, rather than a separation at an arbitrary
boundary location. It excludes the position coordinate of the gap reference
point; that coordinate is represented separately by the [major-radius
coordinate of the plasma-boundary gap reference
point](name:radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Distance between the separatrix and the nearest limiter or wall element

NAMES.name: gap_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed major-radius separation between a measurement
position and the magnetic separatrix after the position is mapped along its
flux surface to the outboard midplane. It applies pointwise to the selected
position and separatrix rather than to an average or to the separation
between two separatrices.

With the mapped position and separatrix evaluated at the outboard midplane,
the separation is defined by

$$
\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} = R_{\mathrm{pos,mid}} - R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}
$$

where $\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the mapped separatrix distance,
$R_{\mathrm{pos,mid}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the mapped
measurement position, and $R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the major-radius
coordinate of the separatrix at the outboard midplane.

The quantity refers to one measurement position, its associated magnetic
flux surface, and one selected separatrix. It is a signed major-radius
separation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with no
flux-surface, spatial, species, or time aggregation. It is not the shortest
geometric distance, a plasma-wall clearance, or the distance between inner
and outer separatrices.

The flux-surface assignment can be expressed through the [normalized
poloidal flux coordinate at measurement position], while the two terms in
the difference are outboard-midplane radial coordinates of the type defined
by [radial coordinate at outboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). The mapping
therefore converts the original position into a common outboard-midplane
comparison before the major-radius difference is taken.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless lower triangularity shape parameter for a nested magnetic flux
surface, given by the normalized inward radial displacement of its lower
vertical extremum.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of a flux surface is the dimensionless triangularity
shape parameter defined at the lower vertical extremum of a nested magnetic
flux surface. It is the normalized inward displacement in major radius $R$
of that lower extremum relative to the magnetic-axis reference.

For the lower vertical extremum, the defining relation is:

$$
\delta_{\mathrm{lower}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{axis}} - R_{\mathrm{lower}}}{a}
$$

where $\delta_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is lower triangularity, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$
is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, $R_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is
the major-radius coordinate of the lower vertical extremum, and $a$ is the
minor radius of the same flux surface. These coordinates are defined in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius
measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$
is vertical height.

This quantity applies independently to each nested magnetic flux surface and
is a geometrical property of the surface rather than a plasma-population
quantity. It resolves the lower vertical extremum only; it is not averaged
over flux surfaces or combined with the upper extremum. It is distinct from
[lower triangularity of a flux surface
boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which describes the
outer plasma boundary rather than an arbitrary nested surface.

It is the lower-extremum branch of [triangularity of a flux
surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), whose parent quantity permits
the relevant upper or lower vertical extremum. The corresponding [upper
triangularity of a flux surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface)
uses the upper vertical extremum, while [elongation of a flux
surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) describes vertical-to-horizontal
shaping rather than triangular displacement.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the lower vertical extremum lies at smaller
major radius $R$ than the magnetic-axis reference, corresponding to an
inward displacement.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless logarithmic radial gradient of the safety factor on a magnetic
flux surface, measuring how magnetic-field-line pitch changes across
neighboring surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at a magnetic flux surface is the local logarithmic radial
variation of the safety factor, expressing the change in magnetic-field-line
pitch between neighboring nested surfaces.

It is defined by

$$
s(\rho_\mathrm{tor}) = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q(\rho_\mathrm{tor})}\frac{dq(\rho_\mathrm{tor})}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $s$ is magnetic shear, $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal-flux radial
coordinate labeling the magnetic flux surface, and $q$ is the safety factor
on that surface.

The quantity applies to the equilibrium magnetic geometry of the specified
magnetic flux surface without restricting the surface to a particular plasma
region, species, or particle population. It is a local value associated with
one surface, not a sum, volume integral, or average over multiple surfaces.

It is distinct from the corresponding values at special loci such as the
[magnetic axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis), [plasma
boundary](name:magnetic_shear_at_plasma_boundary), or [internal transport
barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier). The expression
relates magnetic shear directly to the logarithmic derivative of the safety
factor with respect to the toroidal-flux radial coordinate.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short:
Largest magnitude of the magnetic-field vector over a specified evaluation
domain, distinguishing total field strength from any signed field component.
NAMES.long:
The maximum magnetic-field magnitude is the greatest total field strength
attained within the physical evaluation domain associated with the quantity.

The defining extremum is

$$
B_{\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in D} \left\lVert \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}) \right\rVert
$$

where $B_{\max}$ is the maximum magnetic-field magnitude,
$\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the magnetic-field vector at spatial point
$\mathbf{x}$, and $D$ is the specified evaluation domain.

The domain may be a nested magnetic flux surface or a coil-conductor
surface, as established by the physical context. The maximum operation
aggregates the field magnitude over all points in $D$ and returns its
largest value; it does not represent a spatial average or a particular field
component.

This quantity selects the modulus of the magnetic-field vector before
applying the maximum operation. It is therefore the magnitude-specific child
of [maximum magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field), whose parent
concept leaves the scalar field being maximized unspecified. It excludes
maxima of signed toroidal, poloidal, radial, or other individual
magnetic-field components.

NAMES.name: mhd_energy
NAMES.short:
Global plasma stored energy obtained from the volume integral of total
kinetic pressure, including thermal and fast-particle pressure
contributions.
NAMES.long:
MHD plasma stored energy is the global energy content assigned to the plasma
by integrating its equilibrium-reconstructed total kinetic pressure over the
full plasma volume. It includes thermal and fast-particle contributions
rather than representing only one pressure population.

The defining relation is

$$
W_{\mathrm{MHD}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{MHD}}$ is the MHD plasma stored energy, $p_{\mathrm{tot}}$
is the total kinetic pressure determined by the equilibrium reconstruction,
$V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the complete plasma volume, and $dV$ is the
differential volume element.

This is a global volume-integrated quantity over all included plasma
populations. It is distinct from [thermal plasma
energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which integrates thermal pressure only,
and from [diamagnetic energy](name:diamagnetic_energy), which is restricted
to pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The factor $3/2$
defines the stored-energy convention used for the total kinetic-pressure
integral.

NAMES.name: minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Half the difference between the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates
of the last closed plasma-boundary contour, defining its horizontal
cross-sectional size.
NAMES.long:
The minor radius is the effective horizontal semi-axis of the last closed
plasma-boundary contour and characterizes the radial extent of the plasma
cross-section.

The minor radius $a$ is defined by

$$
a = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $a$ is the minor radius, $R_{\max}$ is the maximum major-radius
coordinate on the boundary contour, and $R_{\min}$ is the minimum
major-radius coordinate on that contour.

This quantity applies to the complete last closed plasma-boundary contour
and is determined from its global major-radius extrema. It is a nonnegative
geometric size parameter, not a local major-radius coordinate such as the
[radial coordinate at the outboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane) and not a
flux-surface average.

The [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary)
uses this minor radius as the horizontal reference semi-axis when forming
the boundary's vertical-to-horizontal shape ratio.

NAMES.name: normalized_plasma_internal_inductance
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless li_3 parameter measuring poloidal magnetic-field peaking
through a plasma-volume integral normalized by total plasma current and a
reference major radius.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the normalized internal inductance of the plasma current
distribution. It characterizes the peaking of the poloidal magnetic field
generated by the total plasma current, rather than a ratio formed only from
a boundary field.

Under the li_3 definition,

$$
l_i = \frac{2}{R_0\mu_0^2 I_p^2} \int_{V_p} B_p^2\,dV
$$

where $l_i$ is the normalized internal inductance, $R_0$ is the reference
major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_p$ is the total signed
plasma current, $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field, $V_p$
is the plasma volume, and $dV$ is a differential volume element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity. The aggregation is a volume integral
of the squared poloidal-field magnitude over the entire plasma volume,
normalized by the square of the total plasma current; it does not select a
separate species, charge state, orbit class, or localized position.

It is distinct from the dimensional [plasma inductance]: the present
quantity includes the reference-radius and vacuum-permeability normalization
in the defining expression and is not a local inductance, a flux-surface
average, or a boundary-field ratio.

If $L_p$ denotes the [plasma inductance], the normalized quantity is related
by $l_i = 2L_p/(R_0\mu_0)$. Thus, under the same reference normalization, a
larger value indicates a more strongly concentrated poloidal-field energy
distribution associated with the plasma current.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_beta
NAMES.short:
Normalized toroidal beta is a dimensionless whole-plasma equilibrium measure
formed from volume-averaged total perpendicular pressure and toroidal
magnetic and plasma-current scales.
NAMES.long:
Normalized toroidal plasma beta, conventionally denoted $\beta_N$, is the
ratio of toroidal plasma beta times plasma minor radius and reference
toroidal magnetic field to total plasma current, including the conventional
factor 100. It is a whole-plasma equilibrium beta metric based on the
volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure entering toroidal beta.

The defining relation is:

$$
\beta_N = 100\,\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}\,\frac{a B_0}{I_p}
$$

where $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta), the
unnormalized toroidal plasma beta; $a$ is the plasma minor radius; $B_0$ is
the reference toroidal magnetic field; and $I_p$ is the total plasma
current. The factor $100$ and the prescribed numerical normalization of $a$,
$B_0$, and $I_p$ are part of the definition.

The scope is the whole plasma. The pressure population is the total
perpendicular plasma pressure represented by $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$, with
the volume averaging inherited from [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta); it
is not restricted to thermal pressure.

This quantity is distinct from [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta), which is
the unnormalized toroidal pressure ratio, and from a thermal-pressure-only
normalized toroidal beta. Within the global beta-metric family, $\beta_N$
rescales [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta) by plasma size,
reference-field, and current factors, whereas
[poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_beta) uses a poloidal-field/current
normalization.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless radial label equal to the square root of toroidal magnetic
flux normalized between the magnetic axis and equilibrium boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate is a dimensionless label for nested
magnetic surfaces, increasing outward from the magnetic axis toward the
equilibrium boundary. It is a magnetic-surface coordinate, not a cylindrical
distance or a local vector component.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the labeled
surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium boundary used
for normalization.

The coordinate applies to nested magnetic surfaces and to mapped physical
locations assigned to those surfaces. It is zero at the magnetic axis and
one at the chosen equilibrium boundary; each value is a single surface
label, with no summation, averaging, species aggregation, or mode
aggregation. Locus-specific quantities such as the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate at a beam-tracing
point](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point) and
the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement
position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position)
are evaluations of this same coordinate.

This quantity is distinct from the dimensionful [toroidal flux
coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate), because it is normalized to the
axis-to-boundary interval and transformed by a square root. It also differs
from the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which uses poloidal
rather than toroidal magnetic flux, and from the [normalized minor radius of
a flux surface](name:normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface), which is
based on geometric extent rather than enclosed toroidal flux.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_absolute_safety_factor
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless magnetic-surface label giving the normalized toroidal flux at
the closed surface where the magnitude of the safety factor reaches its
minimum.
NAMES.long:
This quantity identifies the nested closed magnetic surface on which the
magnitude of the safety factor is minimized, using the normalized toroidal
magnetic-flux coordinate of that surface.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate,
$\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the
evaluated surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic
axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,boundary}}$ is its value at the equilibrium
boundary.

The value is a single equilibrium coordinate evaluated at the surface of
minimum safety-factor magnitude; it is not a flux-surface profile, an
average over surfaces, or the minimum safety-factor value itself. It is
distinct from a cylindrical radial distance and from a local vector
component. The parent [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) supplies the
coordinate definition, while [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum
absolute safety
factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_absolute_safety_factor)
gives the analogous poloidal-flux label at the same physical locus.

NAMES.name: plasma_current
NAMES.short:
Net toroidal electric current carried by the entire plasma column, obtained
by integrating toroidal current density over its enclosed poloidal
cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Plasma current is the net electric current carried by the full plasma
population, represented as the toroidal current crossing a poloidal
cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$
is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

$$
I_p = \int_{A_p} j_\phi\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $I_p$ is the total plasma current, $A_p$ is the enclosed poloidal
cross-sectional area, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the electric
current density, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is the differential area element.

The quantity includes the algebraic sum of toroidal currents from all
charged plasma species and charge states over the complete enclosed plasma
cross-section. It is a global total rather than a local current density, a
species-resolved contribution, or a current restricted to a particular
physical mechanism.

It is the area integral of the toroidal projection of [current
density](name:current_density). The narrower [toroidal total
runaway-electron current](name:toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current)
represents only the runaway-electron contribution and is not the full plasma
current.

of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Pointwise geometric angle locating a position around a magnetic flux-surface
cross-section, measured clockwise from its low-field-side midplane.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle is the geometric angular coordinate assigned pointwise to
each position on the poloidal cross-section of a specified magnetic flux
surface. It is measured from the geometric center of that cross-section
rather than from magnetic-field-line distance.

At a point on the surface, the angle $\theta$ is defined by

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(-(Z-Z_0),\,R-R_0\right)
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the
signed principal angle, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $Z$ is the
vertical coordinate, and $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the geometric center of the
flux-surface cross-section. These coordinates belong to the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

The quantity applies to individual points on one magnetic flux surface and
has no averaging or summation over the surface. The surface is identified by
a constant [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux
surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) value; the angle
therefore parameterizes position around that surface rather than assigning
one unique angle to the entire surface. It is a geometric angle, distinct
from a straight-field-line poloidal angle.

This quantity specializes [poloidal
angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface) by making the flux-surface locus
explicit and provides the angular coordinate used to distinguish positions
around the surface's poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the point advances clockwise from the
low-field-side midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_beta
NAMES.short:
Poloidal beta is a dimensionless measure of total plasma pressure relative
to the magnetic-pressure scale of the plasma-current-generated poloidal
field.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure
content of the confined plasma relative to the magnetic-pressure scale
generated by the plasma current. It characterizes pressure relative to the
poloidal magnetic field rather than the toroidal magnetic field.

The defining relation is

$$
\beta_p = \frac{4\int_V p\,dV}{R_0\,\mu_0\,I_p^2}
$$

where $\beta_p$ is poloidal beta, $p$ is the total plasma pressure, $V$ is
the confined plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $R_0$ is
the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $I_p$ is
the total toroidal plasma current.

The pressure integral extends over the entire confined plasma volume and
aggregates the pressure of all included plasma populations, so this quantity
is global rather than local or species-resolved. It excludes any separate
normalization based on minor radius or reference toroidal magnetic-field
strength.

As the poloidal-field member of the [beta](name:beta) family, poloidal beta
uses a current- and major-radius-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. It
is distinct from [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta), which normalizes
pressure to a toroidal magnetic-field scale, and from
normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta, which applies an additional engineering
normalization.

NAMES.name: poloidal_length_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Poloidal arc length of a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in an
equilibrium poloidal cross-section, measuring the perimeter of that selected
surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one
selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a
geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area,
volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth
parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical
coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at
the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at
fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete
closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple
surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated
with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the
[normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface),
which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the
poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short:
Poloidal magnetic-field strength of the local total induction, formed from
radial and vertical components in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
Local total poloidal magnetic induction is the magnitude of the total
magnetic-field vector projected into the poloidal plane spanned by the
radial and vertical directions. It represents the local poloidal field
strength without selecting a source contribution, perturbation state, or
named evaluation locus.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining
relation is

$$
B_p = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field strength, $B_R$ is the radial
component of the local total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field), and
$B_Z$ is its vertical component. The radial direction follows increasing
$R$, and the vertical direction follows increasing $Z$.

The quantity is pointwise and applies wherever the local total magnetic
induction is defined, including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum. It
has no particle-species or population aggregation and is not spatially
averaged, integrated, or summed over a region. When associated with a
field-sensing location, it denotes the local measured field strength rather
than a value defined as a reconstructed equilibrium estimate.

Unlike the signed [radial magnetic-field
component](name:radial_magnetic_field) and [vertical magnetic-field
component](name:vertical_magnetic_field), this quantity is the nonnegative
magnitude of their combined poloidal projection. Together with the [toroidal
magnetic-field component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), it specifies the
decomposition of the local total magnetic induction into poloidal and
toroidal parts.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux assigned to a nested magnetic surface, serving
as the equilibrium label for its position in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface is the signed magnetic flux through
a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by that
surface. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, it is constant over each nested
magnetic surface and provides its absolute, unnormalized flux label.

The poloidal flux at cylindrical coordinates $(R,Z)$ is defined by

$$
\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is
vertical height, $R'$ is the integration radius, and $B_Z$ is the vertical
magnetic-field component, all expressed in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic surfaces within the
plasma and represents the signed physical flux itself, not a flux-surface
average, species sum, or normalized radial coordinate. It is distinct from
the magnetic flux linked by a [poloidal magnetic flux of a flux
loop](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which is defined by an
oriented diagnostic-loop surface rather than by an equilibrium flux surface.

The [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) is obtained by
shifting and scaling this poloidal-flux label between its magnetic-axis and
plasma-boundary values; the present quantity retains the absolute label.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_Z$ points in the $+Z$ direction through
the integration disk.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the magnetic axis, providing the
inner reference value for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the signed value of the
poloidal flux function at the central extremum associated with nested
magnetic surfaces.

The defining evaluation is

$$
\psi_\mathrm{axis} = \psi(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic
axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function, $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is
the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, and $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is
its vertical coordinate. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is the
[vertical coordinate of the magnetic
axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis).

This quantity applies specifically to the equilibrium magnetic field at the
magnetic axis rather than to an arbitrary point or a plasma region. It is a
single point evaluation with no species selection, regional aggregation, or
flux-surface averaging.

The value is an unnormalized flux reference and is distinct from [poloidal
magnetic flux at the plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which supplies
the outer reference value. Together, these two endpoint values define the
flux interval used by the [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal flux is oriented so that the
vertical magnetic field through the defining horizontal disk points in the
$+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the last closed flux surface,
providing the outer reference for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the signed magnetic
flux through a horizontal disk whose edge lies on the last closed flux
surface. It is the outer boundary value of the poloidal magnetic-flux
function for the confined plasma.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the boundary
value for an axisymmetric equilibrium is

$$
\psi_b = \psi(R_b,Z_b) = \int_0^{R_b} B_Z(R',Z_b)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_b$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary,
$\psi(R_b,Z_b)$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function at a selected
boundary point, $(R_b,Z_b)$ are that point's cylindrical coordinates, $B_Z$
is the vertical magnetic-field component, $R'$ is the integration variable
representing major radius, and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

This quantity applies specifically to the last closed flux surface bounding
the confined plasma. It is a single boundary value of the flux function,
with no averaging over the boundary or enclosed plasma implied; it is
distinct from the value at the magnetic axis given by [poloidal magnetic
flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).

The boundary value supplies the outer endpoint for [normalized poloidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), while the
magnetic-axis value supplies the corresponding inner endpoint. The poloidal
flux function is constant along a given closed flux surface in the
axisymmetric equilibrium description.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_Z$ on the defining horizontal disk points
in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux linked by an individual flux loop, defined by
the magnetic field threading an oriented surface bounded by that loop.
NAMES.long:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux of a flux loop is the magnetic flux linked by
an individual flux loop and threading an oriented surface whose boundary is
that loop. It is the finite-surface flux linkage associated with the loop as
a whole, not a local magnetic-field component.

The loop-linked flux is defined by the surface integral of the
magnetic-field vector over a spanning surface of the loop:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{loop}}} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux of the
flux loop, $S_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is an oriented spanning surface bounded by
the flux loop, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{S}$
is the directed surface element on that surface.

The scope is one specified flux loop and the total flux through its complete
spanning surface; no averaging over multiple loops or loop segments is
implied. The quantity is distinct from a point-locus evaluation such as
[poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment
point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which evaluates a flux
function at a specified position rather than integrating over a finite
loop-bounded surface.

The defining surface is any oriented spanning surface with the same loop
boundary and orientation; the absence of magnetic monopoles makes the linked
flux independent of the particular spanning surface. This quantity is
related to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) as a
loop-bounded flux linkage, and it must not be identified with [toroidal
magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which uses a different
flux-surface geometry; a reconstructed counterpart, [reconstructed poloidal
magnetic flux of flux loop], shares the same magnetic quantity but
represents a distinct value type when that distinction is made.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the magnetic-field vector has a positive net
projection on the oriented surface element selected as positive for the flux
loop.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short:
Geometric area enclosed by a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a
fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ,
Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Geometric area enclosed by a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a
fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame is the poloidal-plane cross-sectional area of that flux
surface. It characterizes the planar section enclosed by one closed magnetic
flux surface.

The area is defined by the planar contour integral

$$
A_{\mathrm{pol}} = \frac{1}{2}\left|\oint_{\mathcal{C}} \left(R\,dZ - Z\,dR\right)\right|
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal-plane cross-sectional area,
$\mathcal{C}$ is the closed poloidal contour of the flux surface at fixed
toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal
symmetry axis, $Z$ is vertical height, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $dR$ and $dZ$ are
differentials along the contour. The absolute value makes the area
independent of the contour traversal orientation.

This quantity applies to the nested family of closed magnetic flux surfaces
from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary; its limiting value at the
magnetic axis is zero. It is an individual-surface geometric measure at
fixed toroidal angle, not an average over toroidal angle, not an aggregate
over multiple flux surfaces, and not a measure of open field-line regions.

It is distinct from the [surface area of flux
surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), which is the area of the
toroidal surface generated by the flux-surface contour. At the last closed
flux surface, the corresponding boundary quantity is the [poloidal-plane
cross-sectional area of plasma
boundary](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary); it
is also distinct from the [volume of flux
surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which measures the toroidal volume
enclosed by the same nested surface.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal plane,
defining the equilibrium plasma cross-sectional size at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic
flux surface (LCFS), which forms the plasma boundary, in a poloidal
cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is
defined by

$$
A_{\rm LCFS} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\rm LCFS}$ is the LCFS cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm
LCFS}$ is the region enclosed by the LCFS contour at fixed toroidal angle
$\phi$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical
height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal-plane area element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity for the complete plasma-boundary
contour. It is not a local surface element, a flux-surface average, or the
area of a toroidal surface formed by revolving the contour.

It is the plasma-boundary specialization of [poloidal plane cross-sectional
area of a flux
surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), whose
corresponding area is defined for an arbitrary closed magnetic flux surface;
the LCFS is the outermost such surface enclosing the plasma.

NAMES.name: product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_of_poloidal_current_function_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Grad–Shafranov equilibrium source term formed by multiplying the poloidal
current function by its derivative with respect to signed poloidal magnetic
flux.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface-dependent product of the poloidal current
function and its derivative with respect to the signed poloidal
magnetic-flux coordinate. It represents the toroidal-field contribution to
the Grad–Shafranov equilibrium source term.

The defining relation is

$$
G(\psi)=F(\psi)\frac{dF(\psi)}{d\psi}
$$

where $G(\psi)$ denotes this quantity, $F(\psi)$ is the [poloidal current
function](name:poloidal_current_function), $\psi$ is the signed poloidal
magnetic-flux coordinate, and $dF/d\psi$ is the derivative of that current
function with respect to $\psi$. The function $F$ is defined by $F=R
B_\phi$, where $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component.

This quantity applies to an axisymmetric equilibrium description on nested
magnetic flux surfaces. It is a local flux-function value with no additional
spatial averaging, species summation, or volume integration. It is distinct
from the poloidal current function itself and from its derivative alone.

Within the Grad–Shafranov balance, this product combines the toroidal-field
contribution with the pressure-gradient contribution to determine the
equilibrium relation for toroidal current density and force balance.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $F$ and $dF/d\psi$ have the same sign for the
chosen orientation of the signed poloidal magnetic flux.

sources.leaf_definition: Derivative of F w.r.t. Psi, multiplied with F

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at its inboard midplane
intersection, locating the high-field-side point relative to the toroidal
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic
flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the
high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry
axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial
coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here,
$R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position
$\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane
intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and
$Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface
at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a
flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding
outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial
coordinate at outboard
midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial
magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the
location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component.

This quantity specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by
fixing the evaluation locus to the inboard midplane. Comparing it with the
outboard-midplane value characterizes the horizontal extent and radial
placement of the same magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the low-field-side intersection between a
magnetic flux surface and the equatorial midplane.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of the point where a
specified magnetic flux surface intersects the equatorial midplane on its
outboard, low-field side. It gives the outboard radial extent of that
surface rather than a distance across the plasma or an average over the
surface.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with unit-vector basis
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, the major-radius coordinate is related to
the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

Here $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis,
$\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, and $x$ and
$y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates measured from that axis.

The quantity applies to one specified magnetic flux surface, identified by
its poloidal magnetic-flux label $\psi$, where $\psi$ denotes the flux
function labeling nested magnetic surfaces. It is evaluated only at the
outboard intersection with the equatorial midplane; it excludes the inboard
intersection and any flux-surface average.

It is a locus-specific specialization of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), obtained by evaluating $R$ at the
outboard midplane. The corresponding [inboard-midplane radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane) describes the
distinct high-field-side intersection of the same type of magnetic surface.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of the designated reference point associated with a
conductor cross-section, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate $R$ assigned to the designated
reference point of a conductor cross-section. It locates the cross-section
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame without describing the
cross-section's shape or extent.

The coordinate is defined from the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the
reference point:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, and
$x$ and $y$ are the horizontal coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical
direction.

The quantity applies to one conductor cross-section and represents one
designated reference location for that cross-section. It is not summed over
conductors, averaged over the cross-sectional area, or resolved pointwise
along the cross-sectional outline.

Unlike the [radial outline of a coil conductor
element](name:radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element), which assigns
radial coordinates to outline points, this quantity identifies the
cross-section's reference geometry. It does not specify the reference
point's vertical coordinate, toroidal angle, dimensions, or outline shape.

This is a conductor-cross-section specialization of the parent [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate); the parent definition supplies the
general major-radius meaning, while this name fixes the locus to a conductor
cross-section.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the midpoint of the plasma boundary's
radial extrema, thereby specifying the horizontal position of its geometric
axis.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the geometric axis is the major-radius position of
the plasma cross-section's geometric center, defined from the extrema of the
plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The geometric-axis coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{geo}} = \frac{R_{\max} + R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric
axis, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major-radius
coordinates of the plasma boundary, respectively.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric axis of the plasma
cross-section and uses the midpoint aggregation of the boundary's radial
extrema. It is distinct from the [radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate)
of an arbitrary point or reference position and from the radial coordinate
of the magnetic axis; its vertical counterpart is the [vertical coordinate
of the geometric axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the magnetic-axis O-point in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame around which nested closed flux
surfaces are organized.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the magnetic axis is the major-radius location of
the O-point, the local extremum of the poloidal magnetic flux around which
nested closed magnetic flux surfaces are organized.

In terms of a right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with
$\hat{z}$ vertical, its major-radius coordinate is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates
perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This is a point value evaluated at the magnetic axis in the plasma poloidal
cross-section; it is not a flux-surface average, region integral, or
coordinate of an arbitrary magnetic or physical contour. It is distinct from
[radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane),
which locates a flux-surface intersection with the inboard midplane.

This quantity is the magnetic-axis specialization of
[radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): the parent applies to general
points or reference positions, whereas this quantity fixes the locus to the
magnetic-axis O-point.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating a measurement position by perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a measurement position is the major-radius location
of that position, defined by its perpendicular separation from the toroidal
symmetry axis. It identifies a single generic measurement location,
independent of the instrument or plasma quantity associated with that
location.

The defining geometric relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{meas}} = \left|\mathbf{r}_{\perp,\mathrm{meas}}\right|
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the measurement
position, $\mathbf{r}_{\perp,\mathrm{meas}}$ is its perpendicular
displacement from the toroidal symmetry axis, and the vertical bars denote
the magnitude of that displacement. The coordinate is expressed in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one measurement position; no averaging, summation, or
integration over positions is implied. This quantity applies to a generic
measurement position and does not identify a particular diagnostic object,
line of sight, toroidal angle, or vertical coordinate. Unlike
[radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight](name:radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight),
it is not restricted to a line-of-sight reference point.

This quantity is the measurement-position specialization of the broader
[radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate); the same perpendicular-distance
definition is used, with the locus narrowed to a measurement position.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short:
Major-radius location of an individual magnetic strike point where a
separatrix leg intersects a divertor target, expressed in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a strike point is its major-radius location
relative to the toroidal symmetry axis, at the intersection of a separatrix
leg with a divertor target.

The major-radius coordinate is defined from the strike point's horizontal
Cartesian position by

$$
R_{\mathrm{sp}}=\sqrt{x_{\mathrm{sp}}^2+y_{\mathrm{sp}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is the strike-point major-radius coordinate, and
$x_{\mathrm{sp}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{sp}}$ are its horizontal Cartesian
coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis,
with $\hat{z}$ vertical and coincident with $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies to one specified magnetic strike point at a time, with
no summation, averaging, or other aggregation. The same definition covers
inner and outer divertor strike points without combining them or selecting
one branch by the name alone.

It excludes the vertical location of the strike point, which is given by the
[vertical coordinate of the strike
point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point). As a component of
[radial_coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), it supplies the major-radius
coordinate needed with the vertical coordinate to locate the strike point in
the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane. The related [radial coordinate of the
X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point) instead identifies the
separatrix's magnetic null rather than its divertor intersection.

sources.parent_definition: Measured or estimated position

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the main X-point, the poloidal
magnetic-field null that defines the separatrix in an equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate of the main X-point is the perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the poloidal magnetic-field null
that defines the separatrix. It identifies the radial location of this
specific equilibrium feature in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame.

The coordinate is defined geometrically by

$$
R_{\mathrm{X}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{X}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{X}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{X}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the main X-point,
and $x_{\mathrm{X}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{X}}$ are its horizontal Cartesian
coordinates in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with
$\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$. The subscript
$\mathrm{X}$ identifies the main X-point.

This quantity applies specifically to the main X-point and represents one
coordinate of that point rather than its complete position. It is a single
geometric value, not an average, integral, or sum over a flux surface or
region; it excludes coordinates of secondary X-points and other equilibrium
features.

It is a locus-specific specialization of the [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), which assigns the same major-radius
concept to arbitrary geometric positions. The X-point condition
distinguishes it from the [radial coordinate of the magnetic
axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), which locates the
poloidal-field O-point rather than the separatrix-defining null.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short:
Rate of change of signed poloidal magnetic flux with the dimensionful
toroidal-flux radius labeling nested equilibrium flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of poloidal magnetic flux is the rate at which the
signed poloidal magnetic flux changes across nested equilibrium magnetic
flux surfaces. It is a metric coefficient relating the poloidal-flux and
toroidal-flux coordinate descriptions.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{d\psi}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux),
and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius that
labels the nested surfaces.

This quantity is evaluated as a function of the toroidal-flux radius, with
one derivative value associated with each nested equilibrium surface. It is
not a surface integral or average, and it is distinct from a derivative with
respect to the cylindrical major radius, minor radius, or a normalized flux
coordinate.

Relative to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), this
quantity describes how the flux label changes in the outward
toroidal-flux-radial direction. It has the same independent coordinate as
the [derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of area of flux
surface], but differentiates poloidal magnetic flux rather than enclosed
surface area.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux increases as
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the
plasma boundary.

sources.leaf_definition: Derivative of Psi with respect to Rho_Tor
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of each point on the plasma-boundary contour in a
poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the major-radius coordinate associated with each point
of the plasma-boundary outline in a poloidal cross-section. It represents
the contour point locations measured from the toroidal symmetry axis rather
than a single representative boundary radius.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the major radius of a
point is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $X$ and $Y$ are horizontal
Cartesian coordinates measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is
the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The quantity is
evaluated pointwise along the plasma-boundary contour, with no averaging or
summation over its points.

It is distinct from a flux-label quantity such as the [normalized poloidal
flux coordinate of the plasma
boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), and
it retains the full radial variation of the contour rather than reducing it
to one size parameter. The radial extrema of the outline provide the
horizontal extent used by the [minor radius of the plasma
boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: RZ outline of the plasma boundary

NAMES.name: reference_major_radius
NAMES.short:
Nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a
designated reference location, serving as the major-radius coordinate where
the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this reference
quantity, the designated location is the radius at which the vacuum toroidal
magnetic field is specified, making it the reference specialization of
major_radius.

At the designated reference location, the major radius is defined
geometrically by:

$$
R_0 = \sqrt{X_0^2 + Y_0^2}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius, and $X_0$ and $Y_0$ are the
Cartesian coordinates of the reference location perpendicular to the
toroidal symmetry axis. The Cartesian basis is right-handed
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$; the corresponding
cylindrical frame is right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ with
$\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.

This quantity is a single designated geometric reference value associated
with the vacuum toroidal magnetic field, represented by [toroidal vacuum
magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field). It is not a pointwise
plasma-radius field, a flux-surface average, or a region integral, and it
has no species or plasma-population scope.

Unlike [flux-surface-averaged major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius), which averages the radius
over a nested magnetic flux surface, this quantity identifies one reference
radius. It is also distinct from a [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) assigned to an arbitrary geometric point
or measurement location.

The reference radius and the vacuum toroidal magnetic field form the
reference pair $R_0$ and $B_0$, where $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic
field specified at the reference radius. Their product $R_0B_0$ supplies the
geometric-field scale used in normalized toroidal-flux and current-density
definitions.
