NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Geometric cross-sectional area enclosed by one winding turn of a poloidal
magnetic-field probe coil, defining its per-turn magnetic-flux coupling.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the geometric cross-sectional area enclosed by one winding
turn of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It represents the
magnetic-flux coupling area of an individual pickup-coil turn and is
nonnegative.

For a winding composed of identical turns, the ideal effective flux-sensing
area is

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = N A_{\mathrm{turn}}
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the signed effective geometric flux-sensing area
of the complete winding, $N$ is the signed number of winding turns, and
$A_{\mathrm{turn}}$ is the area of one turn.

This quantity is defined per turn and applies only to the probe-coil
geometry; it does not include the number of turns, winding orientation, or
calibration factors. Consequently, it is distinct from the complete
effective area of a flux-loop sensor, such as [area of a flux
loop](name:area_of_flux_loop). The corresponding [turn count of a poloidal
magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe)
combines with this area to determine the winding's ideal effective
flux-sensing area.

sources.leaf_definition: Area of each turn of the sensor; becomes effective area when multiplied by the turns
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Geometric area enclosed by one complete winding turn of a toroidal
magnetic-field probe coil, setting its single-turn magnetic-flux
sensitivity.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the geometric area enclosed by one complete winding turn of
a toroidal magnetic-field probe coil. It characterizes the coil’s
single-turn coupling to magnetic flux and is independent of the number of
winding turns.

For a coil with multiple turns, the effective flux-coupling area is related
to the single-turn area by

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = N A_{\mathrm{turn}}
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective flux-coupling area of the complete
winding, $N$ is the signed [turn count of the toroidal magnetic-field
probe](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), and
$A_{\mathrm{turn}}$ is the area enclosed by one turn represented by this
quantity.

The scope is limited to the physical area of one turn of the toroidal
magnetic-field probe coil; no summation over turns, orientation sign, or
additional calibration factor is included. It is distinct from the
corresponding [area of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and from the probe’s
induced [voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), which
results from time-varying linked magnetic flux. Together with the winding
count, this area determines the probe’s magnetic-flux sensitivity.

sources.leaf_definition: Area of each turn of the sensor; becomes effective area when multiplied by the turns
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: length_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Physical extent of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil measured along its
assigned local normal sensing axis, contributing to the coil’s magnetic-flux
response.
NAMES.long:
The length of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the physical extent of its
sensing coil along the coil’s assigned local normal sensing axis. It
describes the coil geometry rather than the length of a signal lead or the
distance between mounting points.

This quantity applies to one poloidal magnetic-field probe coil as a whole.
It is distinct from the [area of the poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), which describes the area
enclosed by one winding turn, and from the [turn count of the poloidal
magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe),
which describes the number and orientation of complete turns.

The coil length, its enclosed per-turn area, and its winding-turn count
jointly characterize the probe’s magnetic-flux coupling and effective
sensing geometry. The length does not itself specify the coil area, winding
count, or magnetic-field orientation.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the sensor along it's normal vector (n)
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: length_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Physical length of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the non-negative axial
extent of the probe coil along its local normal sensing axis. It
characterizes sensor geometry and effective sensing volume; magnetic-flux
sensitivity is associated with enclosed coil area and winding turn count
rather than this length alone.
NAMES.long:
Physical length of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the non-negative axial
extent of the probe coil along its local normal sensing axis. The probe coil
is oriented so that its normal senses the toroidal magnetic-field component
$B_\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the
length refers to sensor geometry, not to an extent of the magnetic field.

Using projection onto the local sensing axis, the length is the span of the
active winding region along that axis:

$$
L_\phi = \max_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{C}} (\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}) - \min_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{C}} (\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})
$$

where $L_\phi$ is the physical length of the toroidal magnetic-field probe,
$\mathcal{C}$ is the active winding region of the probe coil, $\mathbf{r}$
is the position vector of a point in that region, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is
the normalized local normal sensing-axis direction.

This quantity applies to one physical toroidal magnetic-field probe coil; it
is not summed, averaged, or otherwise aggregated over a set of probes. As a
scalar span, it is non-negative and is not a signed displacement along
$\hat{\mathbf{n}}$. It excludes the probe's [enclosed
area](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), winding turn count, body
diameter, lead length, installation position, and any path length around the
device.

The product of this length with the [enclosed
area](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) characterizes the probe's
effective sensing volume. Magnetic-flux sensitivity of the pickup coil is
associated with enclosed area and winding turn count, while the [probe
voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) is the response
quantity produced by changing magnetic flux; the corresponding
[poloidal-probe length](name:length_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) uses
the same projected-span convention for its probe orientation.

sources.leaf_definition: Length of the sensor along it's normal vector (n)
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed poloidal tilt angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s
sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame,
measured clockwise from +R.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed orientation angle of the normal defining a
toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive axis. It specifies the probe’s
tilt in the poloidal cross-section, rather than the spatial angle of the
probe center.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, let $n_R$ and
$n_Z$ denote the components of the probe’s oriented sensitive-axis normal
along the increasing-$R$ and increasing-$Z$ directions. The poloidal angle
$\theta_{\rm pol}$ is defined by:

$$
\theta_{\rm pol} = \operatorname{atan2}(-n_Z,n_R)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ is the two-argument arctangent that preserves
the quadrant of the projected normal.

The scope is one toroidal magnetic-field probe and its oriented
sensitive-axis normal. This is a geometric sensor-orientation quantity, not
the poloidal coordinate of the probe center, the direction of the measured
magnetic field, or a plasma flux-surface coordinate; it has no
plasma-population or region aggregation and is not summed over probes or
coil windings.

It is a probe-specific application of the parent [poloidal
angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface): the parent defines the
geometric angular measure, while this quantity applies it to the probe’s
oriented normal. The complementary
[toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe)
describes the toroidal orientation of the same probe normal, whereas
[poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position)
describes the angular location of a measurement point.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the sensitive-axis normal points from the
outward radial direction toward decreasing $Z$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, following the clockwise direction in the
poloidal plane.

sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the sensor normal vector (vector parallel to the the axis of the coil, n on the diagram) with respect to horizontal plane (clockwise theta-like angle). Zero if sensor normal vector fully in the horizontal plane and oriented towards increasing major radius. Values in [0 , 2Pi]
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed azimuthal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s
sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed toroidal orientation of the sensitive-axis
normal of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It measures the normal’s
departure from the poloidal plane through the orientation of its horizontal
projection.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}} = \operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R), \qquad n_R=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \quad n_\phi=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal orientation angle,
$\mathbf{n}$ is the probe’s sensitive-axis unit normal, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$
are its cylindrical radial and toroidal components, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$
and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are the radial and toroidal unit vectors. Here
$R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height;
$\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the positive radial
direction to the horizontal projection of $\mathbf{n}$.

The quantity applies to the geometric orientation of each poloidal
magnetic-field probe coil. It is not the local plasma magnetic field, a
field component, or an angle averaged over probes, turns, or field samples.
The angle determines how the probe’s sensitive direction is related to the
local magnetic-field vector and therefore how the measured component is
projected. The corresponding toroidal orientation for a toroidal probe is
defined by
[toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe),
while its independent poloidal tilt is represented by
[poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when rotation from the positive radial direction
toward the horizontal projection of the sensitive-axis normal is toward
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the projection of the sensor normal vector (n) in the horizontal plane with the increasing R direction (i.e. grad(R)) (angle is counter-clockwise from above). Values should be taken modulo pi with values within (-pi/2,pi/2]. Zero if projected sensor normal is parallel to grad(R), pi/2 if it is parallel to grad(phi).
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
The toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the signed
azimuthal orientation of the probe sensitive-axis normal projected onto the
horizontal plane, measured from +R toward increasing φ in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. Opposite projected normals are folded into the
same principal orientation.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the signed
azimuthal orientation of the probe sensitive-axis normal after projection
onto the horizontal plane spanned by $\hat R$ and $\hat\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Its zero direction is
the outward radial direction, and the projected normal is treated as an
orientation axis rather than a directed vector.

The angle is defined by the two-argument arctangent of the horizontal normal
components, folded modulo $\pi$ into the principal interval $(-\pi/2,
\pi/2]$:

$$
\alpha_\phi = \mathcal{F}_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2]}\!\left(\operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R)\right)
$$

where $\alpha_\phi$ is this toroidal angle, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are the
radial and toroidal scalar components of the normalized probe sensitive-axis
normal vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and
$\mathcal{F}_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2]}(\beta)$ denotes the representative of an angle
$\beta$ after adding an integer multiple of $\pi$ that lies in $(-\pi/2,
\pi/2]$.

This quantity applies only to toroidal magnetic-field probes and is defined
separately for each probe. It describes sensor orientation, not the
[toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle) that locates a point and not the probe
position; no aggregation over multiple probes is implied.

With the modulo-$\pi$ folding, projections parallel or antiparallel to
$+\hat R$ have $\alpha_\phi=0$, and projections parallel or antiparallel to
$+\hat\phi$ have the principal value $\alpha_\phi=\pi/2$. Together with the
[poloidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field
probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), it specifies
the orientation of the same sensitive-axis normal; it is the
toroidal-field-probe-specific counterpart of the [toroidal angle of a
magnetic-field probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the horizontal orientation is tilted from the
radial basis line toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the projection of the sensor normal vector (n) in the horizontal plane with the increasing R direction (i.e. grad(R)) (angle is counter-clockwise from above). Values should be taken modulo pi with values within (-pi/2,pi/2]. Zero if projected sensor normal is parallel to grad(R), pi/2 if it is parallel to grad(phi).
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed count of complete winding turns in a poloidal magnetic-field probe
coil, fixing the orientation and magnitude of its magnetic-flux linkage.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed number of complete winding turns in a poloidal
magnetic-field probe coil. Its magnitude counts the turns, while its sign
records the winding orientation used to define magnetic-flux linkage.

For turns with a common flux orientation, the total flux linkage is

$$
\Lambda = N\Phi_1
$$

where $\Lambda$ is the total magnetic flux linkage of the coil, $N$ is the
signed winding-turn count, and $\Phi_1$ is the magnetic flux through one
turn using the probe's reference orientation.

This quantity applies to one physical poloidal magnetic-field probe coil and
aggregates all of its complete winding turns, assigning one signed
contribution to each turn. It is a literal coil-turn count, not the local
poloidal magnetic-field value and not the geometric area enclosed by a turn.

For this probe, the literal winding count provides the physical
specialization of the equivalent coupling count represented by
[effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop);
unlike that broader quantity, it is not a homogenized or equivalent
passive-loop count that may be fractional. Together with the
[area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe),
it determines the probe's per-turn magnetic-flux coupling. The corresponding
toroidal-coil quantity is
[turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

sources.leaf_definition: Turns in the coil, including sign
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Signed number of complete winding turns in a toroidal magnetic-field probe
coil, with orientation referenced to the positive toroidal direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed number of complete winding turns in a toroidal
magnetic-field probe coil. It represents the coil's oriented electromagnetic
coupling to the toroidal magnetic-field component, rather than a
magnetic-field value.

The scope is one toroidal magnetic-field probe coil. The count refers to its
physical complete windings, includes their common orientation, and does not
aggregate turns over multiple probes or channels. It excludes the coil's
enclosed area, length, induced voltage, and any calibration factor.

Reversing the winding orientation reverses the sign. Together with the [area
of the toroidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), this count sets the
ideal flux-linkage sensitivity to the toroidal magnetic field. It is the
literal winding-count specialization related to the [effective turn count of
a passive loop](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop), which can
represent equivalent or homogenized windings and may therefore differ from a
complete-turn count. The corresponding poloidal-orientation quantity is the
[turn count of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

The orientation is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

sources.leaf_definition: Turns in the coil, including sign
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Vertical Z coordinate of a position point associated with one flux loop in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the vertical coordinate $Z$ of a position point associated
with one flux loop. It locates that point along the vertical direction in
the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Here $Z$ denotes vertical height, $R$ denotes major radius from the symmetry
axis, and $\phi$ denotes toroidal angle. The value applies to an individual
position point of a single flux loop; it is not a loop-area quantity,
magnetic flux, voltage, or an aggregate over turns, points, or multiple
loops. No population or plasma-region restriction is implied.

Together with the corresponding radial and toroidal position coordinates,
this coordinate locates the flux-loop point in space. It is the
flux-loop-specific counterpart of the [vertical coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), which applies
the same geometric concept to a generic measurement location.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the flux-loop position lies in the +Z
direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the loop (see data structure documentation FLUXLOOPposition.pdf). Leave empty if ../type/index = 6 (differential loop)

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Vertical position of the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe, expressed as its signed Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical position of the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe is the signed height coordinate of the probe center in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It locates the probe center
along the vertical direction and does not define the orientation of the
probe's sensitive axis or the magnetic-field component measured by the
probe.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major
radius from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$
the vertical coordinate, the probe-center coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{probe}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the poloidal
magnetic-field probe center, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the position
vector of that geometric center relative to the coordinate origin, and
$\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector.

This quantity applies to the geometric center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe as a physical object. For a probe with finite extent, it refers to the
center position rather than to the probe size, winding distribution, support
structure, or any spatial average of the measured magnetic field.

Together with the [radial coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), it
specifies the probe-center position in the $(R,Z)$ poloidal cross-section at
a given toroidal angle. The same signed-coordinate concept is used for other
magnetic diagnostic objects, such as the [vertical coordinate of a toroidal
magnetic-field
probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), the
[vertical coordinate of a flux loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop),
and the [vertical coordinate of a Rogowski
coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil), but those names apply to
different objects.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the probe-center position lies above the
machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Vertical position of the geometric center of a toroidal magnetic-field probe
coil, expressed as the signed Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate identifies the geometric center of an individual
toroidal magnetic-field probe coil in the right-handed cylindrical basis
$(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, with coordinates $(R,\phi,Z)$. It locates
the coil and does not represent the magnetic field sensed by the probe.

The coordinate is the projection of the center position onto the vertical
basis direction:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{probe}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{center}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the probe-center vertical coordinate,
$\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{center}}$ is the position vector from the
cylindrical-frame origin to the geometric center of the coil, and $\hat{Z}$
is the vertical unit vector. Here $R$ denotes major radius, $\phi$ denotes
toroidal angle, and $Z$ denotes vertical coordinate.

The quantity applies to one toroidal magnetic-field probe coil center. It is
not summed, averaged, or weighted over windings, probes, or a spatial
region. It excludes the probe's sensitive-axis orientation and the local
magnetic-field value, and is distinct from the corresponding position
coordinate for a [poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

As the $Z$ component of the coil-center position, this coordinate
complements the radial and toroidal position coordinates in locating the
probe within the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the probe-coil center lies in the $+Z$
direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Terminal voltage at a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the inductive voltage
at the coil terminals caused by time variation of the local poloidal
magnetic-field component in the R-Z plane of the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame threading the probe windings.
NAMES.long:
Terminal voltage at a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the signed
coil-terminal electromotive force associated with the probe winding that
senses the local poloidal magnetic field. The sensed field component lies in
the $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and
is projected along the probe sensitive-axis normal.

For a probe with algebraic turn count $N$ and geometric per-turn area $A$,
Faraday's law relates the terminal voltage to the local poloidal field
component $B_p$ as:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_p}{dt}
$$

where $V$ is the terminal voltage at the coil terminals, $B_p$ is the local
poloidal magnetic-field component along the positive sensitive-axis normal,
$N$ is the algebraic turn count including winding direction, $A$ is the
[area of poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), and $t$ is time.

The quantity applies to one poloidal-field probe coil and is not aggregated
over multiple probes. Its locus is specified by the [major radius of
poloidal magnetic-field probe], [toroidal angle of poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), and [poloidal
angle of poloidal magnetic-field probe]; these position quantities identify
where the local field component is sampled and are not themselves voltages.

This quantity is distinct from the derived local poloidal magnetic field. It
is the poloidal-field-probe counterpart of [voltage of toroidal
magnetic-field probe](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), for a
coil oriented to sense the toroidal field, and is distinct from [voltage of
flux loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop), which corresponds to a loop enclosing
magnetic flux rather than a local magnetic-field probe winding.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux threading the coil
in the direction of the probe's positive sensitive-axis normal is decreasing
with time.

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of each geometric point defining a flux-loop
position, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis
in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the non-negative major-radius coordinate $R$ of each
geometric point defining a flux-loop position. In the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is the distance from the toroidal
symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For horizontal Cartesian coordinates $X$ and $Y$ in a right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis whose vertical direction coincides with
cylindrical $\hat{Z}$, the coordinate is defined by:

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $X$ and $Y$ are the point's Cartesian coordinates along $\hat{x}$ and
$\hat{y}$, and $R$ is its major-radius coordinate.

The quantity applies separately to every geometric point defining one
flux-loop position, including a partial loop; it is not a loop-wide average,
centroid, or other aggregation of those points. It is a geometric coordinate
only and does not represent the loop's other position coordinates, linked
magnetic flux, induced voltage, or [effective flux-loop
area](name:area_of_flux_loop).

This quantity is the flux-loop-specific specialization of the general
[radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): it retains the same
major-radius definition while identifying the point as part of flux-loop
geometry. The complete point position requires its corresponding toroidal
and vertical coordinates.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the loop (see data structure documentation FLUXLOOPposition.pdf). Leave empty if ../type/index = 6 (differential loop)

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate locating the center of a poloidal magnetic-field
probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the major-radius
location of the probe center relative to the toroidal symmetry axis,
expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, c6, Z)$ frame.

The coordinate is defined by the magnitude of the displacement perpendicular
to the toroidal symmetry axis:

$$
R = \left|\mathbf{r}_{\perp}\right|
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate and $\mathbf{r}_{\perp}$ is the
displacement from the toroidal symmetry axis within the plane perpendicular
to that axis.

This quantity applies specifically to the geometric center of one poloidal
magnetic-field probe and is not an aggregate over multiple probes or a
coordinate of the measured magnetic field. It identifies the radial location
only; the corresponding vertical location is given by the [vertical
coordinate of the poloidal magnetic-field
probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

It is the probe-specific specialization of the general [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), obtained by evaluating that coordinate
at the probe center.

sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: current_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Signed conventional electric current circulating in one axisymmetric passive
conducting loop, induced by changing linked magnetic flux and
electromagnetic coupling.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the conventional electric current circulating in a single
passive conducting loop. It represents the electromagnetically induced
response of the passive conductor to changing linked magnetic flux,
including transients caused by changing plasma currents, active-coil
currents, disruptions, and coupling to other conductors.

For a passive loop with no separately applied circuit voltage, the linear
circuit response is represented by

$$
\mathcal{R} I(t) + L\frac{dI(t)}{dt} = -\frac{d\Phi_{\rm ext}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $I(t)$ is the loop current, $\mathcal{R}$ is the loop resistance, $L$
is its self-inductance, $t$ is time, and $\Phi_{\rm ext}(t)$ is the
externally linked magnetic flux, including mutual coupling and excluding
flux generated by the loop's own current. The negative sign expresses Lenz's
law.

The quantity applies to one passive conducting loop and denotes its net
circuit current, with all induced contributions aggregated into that loop
current. It excludes current imposed by an external power supply and is
distinct from the current carried by the plasma or by an actively driven
coil. The loop-resolved current contributes to the net [current of a passive
structure](name:current_of_passive_structure) when multiple passive
conducting elements form one structure.

The magnetic coupling and orientation of the loop are interpreted
consistently with its [effective turn
count](name:effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop), whose sign represents the
element orientation relative to positive loop current.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when conventional current circulates in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is
toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

sources.leaf_definition: Passive loop current
sources.parent_definition: Passive axisymmetric conductor description in the form of non-connected loops; any connected loops are expressed as active coil circuits with no power supply attached.

NAMES.name: effective_turn_count_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short:
Signed effective winding count used to weight the magnetic-field
contribution of an individual poloidal-field coil conductor element.
NAMES.long:
The effective turn count is the signed winding multiplicity assigned to one
poloidal-field coil conductor element for calculating its contribution to
the plasma magnetic field. Its magnitude represents the effective number of
turns attributed to that element, while its sign represents winding
orientation.

This quantity applies to an individual conductor element and is not the
total turn count of a complete coil or coil system. It is an effective
electromagnetic contribution rather than a purely geometric count of visible
conductor revolutions, and it excludes the separate winding counts of
magnetic-field probe coils.

For a fixed element current and geometry, the element’s magnetic-field
contribution scales with its effective turn count; reversing the count
reverses the corresponding field contribution. The same signed-winding
concept is used for a [poloidal magnetic-field probe turn
count](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and a [toroidal
magnetic-field probe turn
count](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), although this
quantity applies specifically to a poloidal-field coil conductor element.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of effective turns in the element for calculating the magnetic field from the coil/loop. Should be positive, unless the coil has elements going in opposite directions.
sources.parent_definition: Each PF coil is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually and connected serially

NAMES.name: effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short:
Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent
windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling.
It weights the passive-loop current contribution and may be fractional for
equivalent or homogenized loop elements.
NAMES.long:
Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent
windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling.
It may be fractional when the represented conductor is an equivalent or
homogenized passive-loop element rather than a literal winding.

The signed current-turn source strength represented by the passive loop is
defined by:

$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}} = N_{\mathrm{eff}} I_{\mathrm{loop}}
$$

where $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed current-turn source
strength of the passive loop, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective turn count
of the passive loop, and $I_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the [current of the passive
loop](name:current_of_passive_loop).

This quantity applies to the represented passive loop or passive-loop
element as one electromagnetic circuit contribution. It has no implicit
aggregation over multiple passive loops; if several represented windings or
conductor pieces are collapsed into one loop element, their net orientation
and coupling are represented by the single algebraic value of
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

It is distinct from the [current of the passive
loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is multiplied by
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and from the [area of the passive
loop](name:area_of_passive_loop), which describes conductor cross section.
It is not a turn count for magnetic probes, coil conductor elements,
toroidal-field coils, or magnetic field-line winding.

sources.leaf_definition: Number of effective turns in the element for calculating the magnetic field from the coil/loop. Should be positive, unless the coil has elements going in opposite directions.
sources.parent_definition: Each loop is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually

NAMES.name: height_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Full vertical extent of the rectangular cross-section of one active
poloidal-field coil conductor, measured parallel to Z in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the complete vertical dimension of the rectangular
cross-section of one active poloidal-field coil conductor. It describes the
conductor geometry in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
with the vertical direction parallel to $Z$.

The full height is the difference between the upper and lower vertical
boundaries of the rectangle:

$$
h = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $h$ is the full vertical height, $Z_{\max}$ is the vertical coordinate
of the upper boundary, and $Z_{\min}$ is the vertical coordinate of the
lower boundary.

The quantity applies to the selected poloidal-field-coil conductor and its
rectangular cross-section. It is a complete geometric extent for that
member, not an average, sum, or aggregate over multiple coils or conductor
elements. It is distinct from the radial cross-sectional extent represented
by [width of a poloidal field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and
from the cross-sectional area represented by [area of a poloidal field
coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a rectangular cross-section, this height combines with the corresponding
width to determine the conducting area represented by [area of a poloidal
field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil); the height itself remains the
vertical dimension rather than the full cross-sectional area.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical position of the geometric center of a rectangular conductor
cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed vertical coordinate of the geometric center of
one rectangular conductor cross-section. It locates the rectangle in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius,
$\\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangle with upper and lower vertical boundary coordinates, the
geometric-center coordinate is

$$
Z_c = \\frac{Z_{\\mathrm{top}} + Z_{\\mathrm{bottom}}}{2}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the rectangle center, and
$Z_{\\mathrm{top}}$ and $Z_{\\mathrm{bottom}}$ are the vertical coordinates
of its upper and lower boundaries.

The quantity applies to a single rectangular conductor cross-section,
including a rectangular representation of an axisymmetric magnetic
component. It is not summed or averaged over multiple conductors,
cross-sections, or the conductor's longitudinal extent, and it is distinct
from the rectangle's full vertical extent or area. For coil conductor
elements, its geometric-center meaning is closely related to [vertical
centroid of coil conductor element]; unlike [vertical coordinate of passive
structure], it is tied specifically to the center of a rectangular
cross-section rather than to a generic structure reference point.

NAMES.name: width_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short:
Full radial extent of the rectangular cross-section of one active
poloidal-field coil conductor, measured parallel to the major-radius
coordinate R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Full radial extent of the rectangular cross-section of one active
poloidal-field coil conductor is the scalar side length of that rectangle
parallel to the major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle,
and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity applies to a single active poloidal-field coil conductor whose
cross-section is represented as rectangular. It is the full radial extent of
that one conductor cross-section, with no summation, averaging, or
aggregation over multiple conductors, turns, or coil elements.

It is distinct from the [height of a poloidal-field
coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), which is the full vertical extent
parallel to $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is
also distinct from the [area of a poloidal-field
coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil), a cross-sectional area rather than
a side length, and from any directed displacement or position coordinate.

For the same rectangular conductor cross-section, the [area of a
poloidal-field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) is the product of
this width and the [height of a poloidal-field
coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil).

NAMES.name: vacuum_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short:
Signed major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic field produced by external
coils in an axisymmetric current-free vacuum region.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum poloidal current function is the major-radius-weighted toroidal
magnetic-field component generated by external coils in an axisymmetric
current-free region.

The defining relation is:

$$
F_{\mathrm{vac}}(R,Z) = R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R,Z)
$$

where $F_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum poloidal current function, $R$ is
major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the
toroidal component of the vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame; $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. At a specified
reference major radius, the same invariant is represented as
$F_{\mathrm{vac}}=R_0B_0$, where $R_0$ is the reference major radius and
$B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic field there.

This quantity applies to the combined external-coil contribution in the
axisymmetric current-free vacuum region. It excludes plasma-current and
other non-external-current contributions, is not the total toroidal magnetic
field, and is not a per-coil value or a flux-surface average.

It is the vacuum specialization of the [poloidal current
function](name:poloidal_current_function), which uses the same
major-radius-weighted toroidal-field relation for the relevant equilibrium
field. The [toroidal vacuum magnetic
field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) is the unweighted toroidal
component, while the [difference of vacuum poloidal current function and
initial vacuum poloidal current
function](name:difference_of_vacuum_poloidal_current_function_and_initial_vacuum_poloidal_current_function)
gives its signed change from an initial reference value.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ points in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Vacuum field times major radius in the toroidal field magnet. Positive sign means anti-clockwise when viewed from above
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field coils

NAMES.name: difference_of_vacuum_poloidal_current_function_and_initial_vacuum_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short:
Signed change in the combined external-coil vacuum poloidal current function
relative to its initial reference value, representing variation of the
toroidal field multiplied by major radius.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed difference between the present and initial values
of the vacuum poloidal current function produced by external coil currents.
It represents the change in the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic
field in the axisymmetric current-free vacuum region.

Let $F_{\rm vac}$ denote the [vacuum poloidal current
function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function). Its change relative to the
initial reference state is

$$
\Delta F_{\rm vac}=F_{\rm vac}-F_{\rm vac,initial}=R B_{\phi,\rm vac}-R B_{\phi,\rm vac,initial}
$$

where $\Delta F_{\rm vac}$ is the signed change, $F_{\rm vac}$ is the
present external-coil vacuum poloidal current function, $F_{\rm
vac,initial}$ is its value in the initial reference state, $R$ is major
radius, and $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field
component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $\phi$ is
toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity uses the combined vacuum contribution from external coil
currents and excludes plasma currents and induced currents in conducting
structures. It is a difference from one initial reference value, not the
absolute [vacuum poloidal current
function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function); within an axisymmetric
current-free region, it inherits the parent function's spatial constancy.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the present value of $R B_{\phi,\rm vac}$
exceeds its initial reference value, with $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ positive in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.leaf_definition: Variation of (vacuum field times major radius in the toroidal field magnet) from the start of the plasma.
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field coils

NAMES.name: effective_charge
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless effective ionic charge of a plasma mixture, given by the
second ionic charge moment divided by free-electron density and indicating
impurity content.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ is the charge-weighted mean ionic charge
of a plasma mixture, formed from the second moment of the ionic charge
distribution and normalized by the free-electron density.

The defining relation is

$$
Z_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ions in species and charge-state
category $s$, $Z_s$ is the positive ionic charge number for that category,
and $n_e$ is the free-electron number density. For a quasineutral mixture,
$n_e$ equals the sum of $n_s Z_s$ over the same ion population.

This quantity applies to the complete included ion mixture, with
contributions summed over all represented ion species and charge states; it
is not restricted to one species, charge state, plasma region, or spatial
averaging geometry. A local value and a prescribed spatially averaged value
share this same charge aggregation convention.

Effective charge is distinct from the charge number of an individual ion and
from the [square of an ion charge number](name:square_of_ion_charge_number),
which describes a single-species charge moment rather than the mixture-level
ratio. Spatially averaged instances retain the local definition:
[line-averaged effective charge](name:line_averaged_effective_charge)
averages this quantity along a line, whereas [volume-averaged effective
charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge) averages it over a plasma
volume.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Energy-equivalent measure of the mean random kinetic energy per electron in
the bulk electron population, defined by its second velocity moment.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature is the energy-equivalent measure of random thermal
motion in the bulk electron population. It represents the second moment of
the electron velocity distribution rather than the energy of directed bulk
flow.

For an isotropic electron population, the energy-equivalent temperature is
defined by

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_e \rangle
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature and $\langle E_e \rangle$ is the
population-mean random kinetic energy per electron.

The quantity applies specifically to bulk electrons and is intensive: it is
averaged per electron, not summed over electrons, and excludes ion, neutral,
and directed-flow energies. Without an averaging qualifier, it denotes the
underlying electron-temperature quantity rather than a prescribed chord or
confined-volume aggregate. The [line-averaged electron
temperature](name:line_averaged_electron_temperature) is its path average
along a plasma chord, while the [volume-averaged electron
temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature) is its volume
average over the confined plasma.

It is distinct from [ion charge-state
temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature), which describes the random
kinetic energy of ions in a specified charge state.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short:
Normalized poloidal flux coordinate is a radial label for nested magnetic
flux surfaces based on poloidal magnetic flux. It is zero at the magnetic
axis and one at the last closed flux surface; for a line-of-sight locus, it
denotes the minimum value reached along the line.
NAMES.long:
Normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ is a radial
label for nested magnetic flux surfaces based on the [poloidal magnetic
flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux). It is defined to be $0$ at the magnetic
axis and $1$ at the last closed flux surface, and it identifies the flux
surface associated with a local point, a measurement locus, or a
flux-surface function.

The coordinate is defined from the normalized poloidal-flux difference:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) at
the local point or flux surface being labeled, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the
[poloidal magnetic flux at magnetic
axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and
$\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is the value of poloidal magnetic flux at the last
closed flux surface; all values refer to the same equilibrium.

The supported region is the closed-flux-surface region from the magnetic
axis to the last closed flux surface, giving $0 \le \rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}
\le 1$ for loci in that region. For a local locus, the quantity is the local
value; for a line-of-sight locus, the aggregation convention is the minimum
value attained along the line within the supported region. The line-of-sight
value is not a path average, chord integral, or endpoint value.

The square of $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ is the normalized poloidal-flux
fraction, so the square-root form preserves poloidal-flux surface ordering
while giving a radius-like label. This quantity is distinct from
unnormalized poloidal magnetic flux, from a geometric minor-radius
coordinate, and from the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), which is based on
normalized toroidal magnetic flux rather than normalized poloidal magnetic
flux.

NAMES.name: total_power_due_to_ohmic_dissipation
NAMES.short:
Aggregate rate of irreversible electrical-energy conversion into heat by
resistive current flow across the applicable conducting plasma or structure.
NAMES.long:
Total ohmic-dissipation power is the rate of irreversible conversion of
electrical work into heat by finite-resistivity currents. The total
aggregation covers the complete applicable conducting domain rather than one
selected surface, component, or region.

For a conducting domain $V$, the power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{ohm}} = \int_V \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{res}}\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ohm}}$ is the total ohmic-dissipation power, $\mathbf{J}$
is electric-current density, $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{res}}$ is the resistive
electric field, and $V$ is the conducting volume over which dissipation is
aggregated.

For the global plasma quantity, the domain is the full plasma region and the
result includes the total resistive heating associated with the plasma
current, not only a local contribution or the halo-region contribution. The
same physical definition applies to an explicitly named conducting locus:
[power at the wall](name:power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation) restricts
the domain to wall and vessel structures, while [power of the
divertor](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_ohmic_dissipation) restricts it to
all divertor targets. These locus-specific quantities are distinct from the
global total and exclude radiated or externally launched power.

NAMES.name: coolant_mass_flow_rate
NAMES.short:
Coolant mass throughput across a fluid-flow boundary, representing the rate
at which coolant mass passes through a port or cooling loop.
NAMES.long:
Coolant mass flow rate is the rate of coolant mass crossing a reference
section of a fluid-flow path. It represents fluid throughput for cooling
loops and plant-component ports without selecting one particular physical
location.

The defining mass flow rate is

$$
\dot{m} = \frac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $m$ is the coolant mass
crossing the reference section, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate coolant stream and is not a
volumetric flow rate, coolant temperature, transit time, or thermal power.
The enthalpy transport associated with the flow is
$\dot{m}(h_{\mathrm{out}}-h_{\mathrm{in}})$, where $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the specific enthalpies of the coolant at the outlet
and inlet; the [coolant temperature at
outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) helps characterize the outlet
state. The [coolant transit time of a plant component
port](name:coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port) is a related
elapsed-time quantity, not part of the mass flow rate itself.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when coolant crosses the reference section in the
designated positive flow direction from inlet toward outlet.

NAMES.name: coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port
NAMES.short:
Elapsed time for coolant to traverse the associated plant component from
inlet to outlet, defining the thermal delay between the two coolant states.
NAMES.long:
Coolant transit time is the elapsed travel time for the coolant stream to
pass through the plant component associated with the specified port, from
its inlet to its outlet. It represents the transport delay between the inlet
and outlet thermal states.

The transit time is defined as

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{c}} = t_{\mathrm{out}} - t_{\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the coolant transit time, $t_{\mathrm{in}}$ is
the instant when the coolant crosses the component inlet, and
$t_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the instant when the same coolant stream crosses the
component outlet.

The quantity applies to the coolant path through one associated plant
component and uses the inlet-to-outlet interval as its aggregation
convention. It is not a plant-wide sum over components or ports, and it
excludes transport outside the component, instrumentation or network
latency, and a thermal time constant of the component material.

The transit time establishes the temporal correspondence between inlet
conditions and the delayed outlet state represented by the [coolant
temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet). It is distinct
from the [coolant mass flow rate](name:coolant_mass_flow_rate), which
describes transported mass per time rather than travel duration, and it
provides the thermal-delay correction relevant to [total thermal coolant
absorbed power at wall](name:total_thermal_coolant_absorbed_power_at_wall).

NAMES.name: ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short:
Collected conventional electrical current carried by the ion population
assigned to one mass-resolved channel.
NAMES.long:
The collected ion current is the conventional electrical current delivered
to a detector by ions assigned to one selected atomic-mass or mass-to-charge
channel. It represents the channel-specific ion population rather than the
complete detector signal across all mass channels.

The defining charge-collection relation is

$$
I_{\mathrm{ion}} = \frac{dQ_{\mathrm{ion}}}{dt} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{C}} q_k\frac{dN_k}{dt}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the collected ion current, $Q_{\mathrm{ion}}$ is
the charge delivered by collected ions, $t$ is time, $\mathcal{C}$ is the
set of ion populations assigned to the selected channel, $q_k$ is the charge
carried by an ion in population $k$, and $N_k$ is the cumulative number of
ions from population $k$ collected by the detector.

The aggregation is over all ion arrivals assigned to the selected channel
and species, including any charge states represented by that channel; it is
not an aggregate over the full mass spectrum or over unrelated channels. The
quantity excludes neutral-gas pressure and the detector-bias potential
represented by the [voltage of a mass-spectrometer
channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

Unlike [ion current density](name:ion_current_density), which is a local
vector charge flux per area, this quantity is the total collected current
associated with one channel. Its channel-specific value can therefore
contribute to determining the corresponding species abundance, while
remaining distinct from a current density.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when positive ion charge is collected by the
detector channel.

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short:
Azimuthal position of an aperture’s geometric center around the machine
symmetry axis, measured as the toroidal angle in the right-handed (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate of an aperture is the azimuthal angle locating the
geometric center of a collimating aperture about the machine symmetry axis.
It identifies the aperture’s toroidal placement in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ increases with toroidal
angle.

For Cartesian coordinates of the aperture center in the plane perpendicular
to the symmetry axis, the toroidal angle is defined by

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the center coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian
$(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angular
coordinate. The angular origin and equivalent $2\pi$ representation follow
the adopted toroidal-angle convention.

This quantity applies to the geometric center of one aperture. For a
circular aperture, the center is the circle center; for a planar aperture,
it is the origin of the local coordinate system describing the aperture
plane. It is not an area average, a boundary coordinate, or the toroidal
coordinate of a measurement position along the associated line of sight.

Together with the corresponding radial and vertical center coordinates, it
locates the aperture in space. The same geometric convention is used for the
[toroidal coordinate of an optical
element](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element) and the [toroidal
coordinate of a camera](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_camera), which locate
other diagnostic components by their geometric centers.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Signed bias potential applied between the photomultiplier detector electrode
and its electronics reference for one mass-resolved channel, setting
ion-signal gain.
NAMES.long:
The mass-spectrometer channel voltage is the detector-bias potential
difference associated with one channel assigned to a selected atomic mass.
It is an instrumental operating parameter of the photomultiplier detector
that controls the gain applied to the collected ion signal, rather than a
plasma thermodynamic or field quantity.

The defining potential difference is

$$
V_{\mathrm{ch}} = \phi_{\mathrm{det}} - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the channel detector-bias voltage,
$\phi_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the electric potential of the photomultiplier
detector electrode, and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the electronics reference
potential.

This quantity applies to one mass-resolved channel and its associated
detector circuit. It is not summed or averaged across channels, mass
assignments, detector electrodes, or ion populations, and it does not
represent a local plasma voltage.

The channel-level quantity specializes the device-level [mass-spectrometer
detector bias voltage](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer) to one channel. It
is distinct from the [ion current of a mass-spectrometer
channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel), which is the
collected electrical signal, and from the [voltage of a spectrometer
channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel), which denotes an electrical
output signal rather than the detector-bias potential.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the detector electrode potential exceeds the
electronics reference potential.

sources.leaf_definition: Voltage applied to the photomultiplier

NAMES.name: line_averaged_effective_charge
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless line-averaged effective ionic charge of a plasma mixture,
obtained by averaging local effective charge along a prescribed plasma line
of sight.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged effective ionic charge characterizes the charge composition of
a plasma mixture through the average of its local effective charge along a
prescribed line of sight.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{L} \int_{0}^{L} Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\overline{Z}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the line-averaged effective ionic
charge, $L$ is the total path length through the plasma, $\ell$ is distance
along the line of sight, and $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}(\ell)$ is the local effective
charge at position $\ell$.

This quantity applies to the complete included ion mixture along the line of
sight. At each position, the ionic contribution is summed over all
represented ion species and charge states, while the line aggregation is a
uniform average over physical path length.

The local integrand is the [effective charge](name:effective_charge),
defined from the second ionic charge moment divided by free-electron
density. This quantity is distinct from a local effective charge at a single
position and from the [volume-averaged effective
charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge), which uses volume weighting
rather than line-of-sight path-length weighting; it also differs from the
[flux-surface-averaged effective charge at the plasma boundary], which
averages over a boundary surface.

sources.leaf_definition: Average effective charge along the line of sight
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

sources.leaf_definition: Ionic effective charge, line average along the channel line-of-sight

NAMES.name: accumulated_coolant_absorbed_energy_of_calorimetry_component
NAMES.short:
Cumulative thermal energy transferred from a calorimetry component to its
coolant since pulse start, determined from the coolant enthalpy gain.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cumulative thermal energy extracted from a calorimetry
component and carried away by its associated coolant between pulse start and
the evaluation time.

The accumulated energy is defined by the time integral of the coolant
enthalpy gain:

$$
E_{\mathrm{abs}}(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{m}_{\mathrm{c}}(t')\left[h_{\mathrm{out}}(t') - h_{\mathrm{in}}(t')\right] \, dt'
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)$ is the coolant-absorbed energy at evaluation
time $t$, $t_0$ is pulse start, $t'$ is the integration time,
$\dot{m}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the coolant mass flow rate associated with the
component, and $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the coolant
specific enthalpies at the component outlet and inlet, respectively.

The quantity applies to the coolant associated with the calorimetry
component and represents the total accumulated enthalpy transfer over the
full interval from $t_0$ to $t$, rather than an instantaneous power or a
local heat flux. It excludes thermal energy retained within the component.

Differentiation with respect to $t$ gives the corresponding coolant-absorbed
power. The same cumulative coolant-transfer concept evaluated specifically
for a plasma-facing component is [coolant-absorbed energy accumulated of a
plasma-facing
component](name:coolant_absorbed_energy_accumulated_of_plasma_facing_component);
this quantity retains the broader calorimetry-component locus.

sources.leaf_definition: Energy extracted from the component since the start of the pulse
sources.parent_definition: Set of components on which calorimetry measurements are carried out

NAMES.name: accumulated_total_gas_count
NAMES.short:
Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species delivered by
injection after plasma breakdown, summed across species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of gas
introduced into the plasma by injection after plasma breakdown. It combines
all injected gas species into one total inventory.

The total is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s z_s N_s(t)
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $s$
identifies an injected gas species, $N_s(t)$ is the cumulative number of
particles of species $s$ delivered since plasma breakdown, and $z_s$ is the
equivalent-electron contribution per particle; for an atomic species, $z_s$
is its atomic number, while for a molecule it is the sum of the atomic
numbers of its constituent atoms.

The quantity applies to all gas species and uses a cumulative sum over the
post-breakdown injection history. It excludes gas introduced during prefill
before plasma breakdown, instantaneous injection rates, and any
single-species inventory such as [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas
injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection).

It is the post-breakdown counterpart of the prefill inventory [accumulated
total prefill gas count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count); the two
quantities differ by the injection phase they accumulate.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total accumulated injected gas (sum over species)

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_inlet
NAMES.short:
Absolute thermodynamic temperature of coolant entering a cooling loop or
plant component, establishing the upstream state for enthalpy-based
heat-transfer balances.
NAMES.long:
The coolant inlet temperature is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of
the coolant or working fluid at the entrance to a cooling loop, plant
component, or cooling module. It specifies the upstream thermal state of the
fluid before heat transfer through the associated cooled volume.

The quantity is a local boundary value at the relevant inlet and is not an
average or aggregate over multiple components, loops, or inlet streams. It
applies to the coolant population crossing that inlet, rather than to the
cooled solid or the plasma.

It is distinct from the downstream [coolant temperature at
outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) and does not represent the
temperature change across the cooled component or loop.

In an enthalpy balance, the inlet temperature supplies the upstream thermal
state and is used with the outlet temperature and [coolant mass flow
rate](name:coolant_mass_flow_rate) to determine thermal power transferred to
the coolant. The quantity itself is a temperature, not a power or a
coolant-flow measurement.

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_outlet
NAMES.short:
Absolute thermodynamic temperature of coolant leaving a cooling component or
loop, specifying the fluid’s outlet thermal state for enthalpy-based heat
balance.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the coolant fluid
at the outlet of a cooling component, cooling loop, or comparable coolant
circuit. It describes the bulk fluid state at the exit boundary.

The scope is limited to coolant at an outlet and does not represent the
inlet temperature, a wall temperature, or an aggregate temperature over the
entire cooling system. It is an outlet state value for the selected cooling
path, not a mass-flow rate or a deposited-power quantity.

Together with the [coolant temperature at the
inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) and the [coolant mass flow
rate](name:coolant_mass_flow_rate), this temperature determines the coolant
enthalpy change used to assess heat transferred into the fluid. The enthalpy
balance distinguishes thermal power deposited in the coolant from the outlet
temperature itself.

NAMES.name: total_neutral_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Instantaneous equivalent-electron source rate of neutral gas introduced into
the vessel by gas injection, summed over all injected species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the instantaneous neutral-gas throughput supplied to the
vessel by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron rate. It
combines all injected neutral species rather than representing one gas
species.

For the set of injected species, the equivalent-electron rate is defined by:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} Z_s\,\dot{N}_s
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the total equivalent-electron source rate,
$\mathcal{S}$ is the set of injected neutral gas species, $\dot{N}_s$ is the
particle injection rate of species $s$, and $Z_s$ is the equivalent-electron
weighting per injected particle. For an atomic species, $Z_s$ is its atomic
number; for a molecule, it is the sum of the atomic numbers of its
constituent atoms.

The quantity applies to the vessel-level gas input and is aggregated by
summing over all injected neutral species. It is an instantaneous rate, not
a time-integrated inventory, and excludes ionization and subsequent plasma
particle sources. Species-resolved rates such as the [hydrogen source rate
due to gas injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection)
provide individual contributions to this total. Unlike the [total lower gas
source rate of the vacuum vessel due to gas
injection](name:total_lower_gas_source_rate_of_vacuum_vessel_due_to_gas_injection),
it is not restricted to the lower vessel region.

The corresponding accumulated quantity, such as the [accumulated hydrogen
count due to gas injection], is obtained by time integration and represents
delivered inventory rather than instantaneous throughput.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total gas injection rate (sum over species)

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate R locating each point on the boundary outline of a
plasma-facing limiter tile in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate is the major-radius value $R$ of each point on
the geometric boundary outline of a plasma-facing limiter tile. It describes
tile geometry rather than a plasma field or a flux-surface coordinate.

In a right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the major-radius
coordinate is defined from Cartesian coordinates by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, and
$x$ and $y$ are Cartesian coordinate values along the $\hat{x}$ and
$\hat{y}$ axes of the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis.

The quantity is evaluated pointwise for every contour point of the
limiter-tile outline. It is not an average, maximum, area, or integrated
boundary measure; for a closed contour, the first point is not repeated at
the end.

Together with the [vertical outline of the limiter
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), it supplies the complementary
radial and vertical coordinates that locate the outline in a poloidal
cross-section. The related [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate)
expresses the same geometric coordinate concept without specifying the
limiter-tile outline locus.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_wall
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate is the major-radius position of each point on
the boundary contour designated as the wall. It locates the contour relative
to the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical coordinate.

For a contour point identified by parameter $s$, the coordinate is defined
by

$$
R(s)=\mathbf{r}(s)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}(s)
$$

where $\mathbf{r}(s)$ is the position vector of the contour point measured
from the machine symmetry axis, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}(s)$ is the local outward
radial unit vector, and $s$ identifies the point along the outline.

The quantity applies point-by-point to the specified wall contour and
carries no contour averaging, integration, maximum, or other spatial
aggregation. The generic wall locus does not by itself distinguish a first
wall, vacuum-vessel wall, or limiter surface; that physical boundary
identity is determined by the applicable wall definition. It is a radial
coordinate, not a vertical coordinate, toroidal coordinate, surface-normal
coordinate, or wall-normal distance.

Its meaning is analogous to [radial outline of a limiter
tile](name:radial_outline_of_limiter_tile), but the evaluated boundary
differs; [radial outline of a coil conductor
element](name:radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element) likewise applies the
same radial-coordinate concept to a conductor contour rather than a wall
contour.

sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the mobile unit, for a set of time slices. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: area_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short:
Geometric area of the designated diagnostic aperture surface that admits or
collects radiation or particles.
NAMES.long:
Diagnostic aperture area is the geometric extent of the designated limiting
surface through which radiation or particles are admitted or collected. It
may describe a clear aperture opening or a collecting face when that face
defines the aperture.

The area is defined by the surface integral

$$
A = \int_S dS
$$

where $A$ is the diagnostic aperture area, $S$ is the designated aperture
surface, and $dS$ is the differential area element on that surface.

This quantity applies to the specified aperture surface of the diagnostic
and is not an automatically aggregated area for unrelated apertures. It is a
geometric area, excluding surrounding housing, supports, and other
structures unless they form the designated aperture surface; it is not an
effective area weighted by transmission, sensitivity, or angular response.

The area is distinct from the [radius of a diagnostic
aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) and the [width of a diagnostic
aperture], which describe linear dimensions. For a circular aperture of
radius $r$, where $r$ is the geometric distance from the aperture center to
its boundary, the area satisfies $A = \pi r^2$, with $\pi$ denoting the
circle constant.
