NAMES.name: cold_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless fraction of the cold recycled component of a hydrogen-isotope
neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The cold neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$
expressing the relative abundance of the cold, low-energy recycled component
of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader
[neutral
fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density),
distinct from the hot charge-exchange-born component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{cold}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{cold}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the cold neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$
is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms, and $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$
is the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the
two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral
population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not
summed across different isotopes and does not represent the hot component
itself.

Within this model, the cold and hot fractions are complementary and sum to
unity. The [hot neutral fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) gives the
corresponding charge-exchange-born component, with the energy threshold
separating the two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of cold neutrals for this isotope (n_cold_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: etendue_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Geometric optical throughput of a hard X-ray detector’s optical system,
determined by its effective collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Étendue is the geometric throughput of the optical system associated with a
hard X-ray detector. It characterizes the angular and spatial acceptance
that determines how incident radiation is coupled into the detector.

The defining relation is

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $G$ is the detector étendue, $A$ is the effective collecting area, and
$\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle.

This quantity applies to the detector-level optical system and uses
effective area and angular acceptance for the associated detector; it does
not specify whether those properties arise from one or multiple optical
elements. It is distinct from the detector’s linear dimensions, such as its
[height](name:height_of_hard_xray_detector) and width, which do not
determine optical throughput alone.

Étendue provides the geometric factor relating incident [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) to radiation coupled into the
detector and is the same physical optical-throughput concept represented by
[etendue_of_spectrometer](name:etendue_of_spectrometer), with the owning
optical system changed from a spectrometer to a hard X-ray detector.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: etendue_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Geometric optical throughput of a soft X-ray detector channel, set by the
collecting area and accepted solid angle of its optical system.
NAMES.long:
Etendue is the geometric throughput of the complete optical system serving a
soft X-ray detector channel. It characterizes the channel's acceptance of
radiation by combining its collecting area with the range of accepted
propagation directions.

For the channel optical system, etendue $G$ is defined by

$$
G = A\Omega
$$

where $A$ is the effective collecting area of the detector or aperture and
$\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle subtended by that area.

This quantity applies to the specified soft X-ray detector channel and
represents the geometric optical factor for that channel as a whole. It
excludes the radiation radiance, spectral response, detector conversion
efficiency, and other non-geometrical response factors.

The same geometric throughput concept is used for other diagnostic systems,
including [hard X-ray detector etendue](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector)
and [bolometer etendue](name:etendue_of_bolometer); those quantities differ
by the owning diagnostic object rather than by the defining relation.

sources.leaf_definition: Etendue (geometric extent) of the channel's optical system
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hard_xray_brightness
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short:
Band-integrated hard X-ray photon radiance received by a channel, normalized
by projected collecting area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Hard X-ray brightness is the photon radiance received from a viewing
direction by a channel. It represents photon arrival rate with the
photon-energy dependence integrated over the selected hard X-ray band.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by

$$
B_{\mathrm{HX}} = \frac{dN_\gamma}{dt\,dA_{\mathrm{proj}}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{HX}}$ is the hard X-ray brightness, $N_\gamma$ is the
number of received photons in the selected energy band, $t$ is time,
$A_{\mathrm{proj}}$ is projected collecting area, and $\Omega$ is accepted
solid angle.

This quantity applies to hard X-ray photons received by a channel and is
evaluated separately for each selected energy band. Its aggregation
convention is integration over photon energy within that band while
retaining normalization by projected area and solid angle. It is a received
radiometric quantity, not a local volumetric source term, and it counts
photons rather than their deposited or carried energy.

The local production counterpart is [hard X-ray emissivity], which describes
photon generation per unit volume and solid angle before propagation to the
channel. Integrating this brightness over the collecting geometry
represented by the [etendue of a hard X-ray
detector](name:etendue_of_hard_xray_detector) gives the received photon rate
under the corresponding angular and area acceptance. Unlike [incident soft
X-ray radiance](name:incident_soft_xray_radiance), which is energy-weighted,
this quantity is photon-count radiance; photon registration probability is a
separate detector property described by [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector).

sources.leaf_definition: Photons received by the detector per unit time, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. photon flux divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hard_xray_emissivity
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short:
Local production rate of hard-X-ray bremsstrahlung photons per plasma volume
and emission solid angle, integrated over a specified photon-energy band.
NAMES.long:
Hard-X-ray emissivity is the local bremsstrahlung photon production rate per
plasma volume and emission solid angle, integrated over the selected
hard-X-ray photon-energy band. It represents emission from suprathermal
electrons at a physical location and in a specified emission direction.

The band-integrated emissivity is defined by

$$
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}(\mathbf{r},\Omega;E_1,E_2)=\int_{E_1}^{E_2}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}(\mathbf{r},\Omega,E)\,\mathrm{d}E
$$

where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}$ is the band-integrated hard-X-ray photon
emissivity, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}^{(E)}$ is the differential photon
emissivity with respect to photon energy, $\mathbf{r}$ is the emission
location, $\Omega$ is the emission direction labeled by solid angle, $E$ is
photon energy, and $E_1$ and $E_2$ are the lower and upper limits of the
selected energy band.

This quantity is local and directional: it is not integrated along a line of
sight, over a plasma volume, or over emission directions. It applies to
hard-X-ray photons produced by suprathermal-electron bremsstrahlung and
excludes the total bremsstrahlung electromagnetic power and
detector-received radiation.

In an optically thin plasma, [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness) is obtained from the corresponding
local emissivity by propagation and integration along a viewing path;
brightness is therefore a received radiance, whereas this quantity is the
local photon source density.

sources.leaf_definition: Radial profile of the plasma emissivity in this energy band
sources.parent_definition: Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless fraction of the hot charge-exchange-born component of a
hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom
population.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$
expressing the relative abundance of the hot, charge-exchange-born component
of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader
[neutral
fraction](name:ratio_of_neutral_state_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density),
distinct from the cold recycled component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{hot}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{hot}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the hot neutral fraction, $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is
the number density of hot charge-exchange-born neutral atoms, and
$n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms.

The quantity applies to a specified hydrogen isotope and uses the
two-component neutral-population model. Its denominator is the total neutral
population formed by the cold and hot components for that isotope; it is not
summed across different isotopes and does not represent the cold component
itself.

Within this model, the hot and cold fractions are complementary and sum to
unity. The [cold neutral fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) gives the
corresponding recycled component, with the energy threshold separating the
two components defined by the applicable population model.

sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of hot neutrals for this isotope (n_hot_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: incident_soft_xray_radiance
NAMES.short:
Incident soft X-ray power radiance gives received electromagnetic power per
projected detector area and solid angle, integrated over the selected energy
band.
NAMES.long:
Incident soft-X-ray power radiance is the energy-integrated radiant power
arriving at a receiving surface from the viewing direction, expressed per
projected area and per solid angle.

$$
L_{\rm inc} = \int_{\mathcal{E}} L_E^{\rm inc}\,dE = \frac{dP_{\rm inc}}{dA_\perp\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\rm inc}$ is the incident power radiance, $L_E^{\rm inc}$ is the
incident spectral power radiance at photon energy $E$, $\mathcal{E}$ is the
selected photon-energy band or collection of bands, $P_{\rm inc}$ is
incident radiant power, $A_\perp$ is projected receiving area, and $\Omega$
is accepted solid angle.

The quantity applies to soft X-ray radiation incident on a detector channel,
with spectral dependence integrated over the selected energy band or bands.
It is an incoming radiometric quantity per area and solid angle, not a total
power integrated over the detector aperture or viewing directions, and it is
distinct from detector-registration efficiency.

Integrating this radiance over the relevant projected area and solid angle
gives the band-integrated received power represented by [power of soft X-ray
detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). Unlike [hard X-ray
brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which is photon-number radiance,
this quantity is power radiance; [spectral efficiency of soft X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector) instead describes
the probability that incident photons are registered.

sources.leaf_definition: Power flux received by the detector, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. power divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector

NAMES.name: intensity_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Uncalibrated photoelectron detection rate obtained by integrating the
measured emission signal across an identified spectral line.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the uncalibrated photoelectron count rate associated with
one identified emission line. It represents the detector signal integrated
across the wavelength interval assigned to that line, rather than an
absolutely calibrated photon radiance.

The line-integrated count rate is defined by

$$
I_{\rm line} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} i(\lambda)\,d\lambda
$$

where $I_{\rm line}$ is the integrated photoelectron count rate,
$i(\lambda)$ is the spectral photoelectron count-rate density, $\lambda$ is
wavelength, and $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ delimit the interval assigned to
the identified emission line.

The quantity applies to a single identified spectral line and uses line
integration as its aggregation convention. It is non-calibrated and is not
background-subtracted; no aggregation over multiple spectral lines or
conversion to absolute photon radiance is included.

It is the uncalibrated line-integrated counterpart of [photon-count radiance
at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), which
additionally represents an absolutely calibrated radiance and includes
background subtraction. Unlike [spectral flux of a spectrometer
channel](name:spectral_rate_of_spectrometer_channel), this quantity is
resolved at one identified line rather than describing the channel-level
spectral signal.

sources.leaf_definition: Non-calibrated intensity (integrated over the spectrum for this line)
sources.parent_definition: Set of processed spectral lines

NAMES.name: lower_bound_photon_energy
NAMES.short:
Lower boundary of an X-ray photon-energy band, specifying the minimum photon
energy included in the defined detection or emission band.
NAMES.long:
Lower boundary of an X-ray photon-energy band is the minimum photon energy
included in the specified detection or emission band. It defines the
low-energy cutoff of that band.

The photon-energy band defined by this lower boundary and its complementary
upper boundary satisfies:

$$
E_\mathrm{low} \le E \le E_\mathrm{up}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{low}$ is the lower-bound photon energy, $E$ is the photon
energy being classified, and $E_\mathrm{up}$ is the [upper photon
energy](name:upper_photon_energy).

The scope is an X-ray spectral band for photon detection, photon counting,
or energy-resolved emissivity. This quantity is a band boundary, not an
observed photon energy, photon-energy width, photon flux, count rate,
emissivity, or detector-response amplitude; it is a single boundary for one
specified band and implies no averaging or summation over photons.

Together with the [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy), it
specifies the spectral interval of the band. The lower boundary must not
exceed the upper boundary, and any derived band width is their difference.

NAMES.name: lower_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short:
Lower wavelength of a filter is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum
wavelength, that identifies the short-wavelength boundary of a diagnostic
filter's transmitted spectral band.
NAMES.long:
Lower wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength spectral coordinate
that identifies the short-wavelength boundary of a diagnostic filter's
transmitted spectral band. It marks the high-photon-energy edge of the
interval selected by the filter transmission response.

For a lower-bound characteristic associated with temporal frequency
$\nu_\mathrm{lower}$, the vacuum wavelength is defined by:

$$
\lambda_\mathrm{lower} = \frac{c}{\nu_\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $\lambda_\mathrm{lower}$ is the lower filter-boundary vacuum
wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_\mathrm{lower}$ is
the temporal frequency corresponding to that boundary.

This quantity applies to the transmitted spectral band of the filter and is
a single lower-edge value, not a wavelength average, an integrated spectral
quantity, or the complete transmission function. It is distinct from a
spectral-line rest wavelength and from a wavelength defined inside a
material medium.

As the lower-bound member of [wavelength of a
filter](name:wavelength_of_filter), it identifies one characteristic point
of the filter response. Together with the [upper wavelength of a
filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), it defines the passband span
represented by the [width of a filter].

NAMES.name: photon_radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Photon-count radiance from an identified emission transition, integrated
over its spectral line interval and resolved by projected area and viewing
solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Photon-count line radiance is the photon emission rate from one identified
transition accumulated along the emitting line of sight, resolved by
projected collecting area and viewing solid angle.

The defining photon-count radiance is

$$
L_{\gamma,\ell} = \frac{d^3 N_{\gamma,\ell}}{dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the line radiance, $N_{\gamma,\ell}$ is the
number of photons from transition $\ell$, $\ell$ identifies the emission
transition, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is collecting area projected normal to
the viewing direction, and $\Omega$ is viewing solid angle.

The quantity applies to one identified emission transition without imposing
a particular emitting species, charge state, or line-splitting mechanism.
Photon counts are integrated across the selected spectral-line interval and
accumulated along the viewing path; the result is not resolved per
wavelength.

Integrating [photon-number spectral radiance] over wavelength across the
selected line interval gives this line radiance under matching
projected-area and solid-angle conventions. The qualified [motional-Stark
photon radiance at a spectral line] is a specialized instance restricted to
an identified motional-Stark-split component. Unlike energy radiance, this
quantity counts photons without weighting them by photon energy; conversion
to energy radiance requires applying that energy weighting before
integration.

NAMES.name: power_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Band-integrated radiant power received by a soft X-ray detector channel over
its selected photon-energy band or bands.
NAMES.long:
Soft X-ray detector power is the radiant power carried by incident soft
X-ray photons and received by one detector channel after spectral selection.
It represents radiation power rather than the detector’s electrical output.

For a selected photon-energy band, the received power is defined by:

$$
P_{\mathcal{B}} = \int_{\mathcal{B}} E\,\Phi_E(E)\,dE
$$

where $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ is the received power for band $\mathcal{B}$, $E$ is
photon energy, $\Phi_E(E)$ is the photon arrival-rate density as a function
of photon energy, $\mathcal{B}$ is the selected energy interval, and $dE$ is
an infinitesimal photon-energy interval.

The quantity applies to soft X-ray radiation received by a particular
detector channel and is integrated over photon energy within its selected
bandpass. It is not summed over detector channels, viewing directions, or
distinct energy bands; when multiple bands are resolved, each band has its
own band-integrated received-power value. It excludes plasma-emitted power
before arrival at the detector and electrical power generated by detector
electronics.

The quantity is distinct from
[spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector),
which describes the probability of registering an incident photon rather
than the received radiant power. It is also distinct from
[hard_xray_brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which describes photon
radiance rather than the power collected by a channel over its energy band
and collection geometry.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_over_core_region
NAMES.short:
Total electromagnetic power radiated by plasma inside the last closed flux
surface, representing the core-region contribution to global radiative
energy loss.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power over the core region is the total electromagnetic energy-loss
rate carried away by radiation emitted within the plasma volume inside the
last closed flux surface (LCFS). It is a regional integral rather than a
local radiated-power density.

The defining volume integral is

$$
P_{\rm core} = \int_{V_{\rm core}} p_{\rm rad}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\rm core}$ is the core-region radiated power, $p_{\rm
rad}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local volumetric radiated-power density at position
$\mathbf{r}$, $V_{\rm core}$ is the plasma volume inside the LCFS, and $dV$
is the differential volume element.

The quantity includes the aggregate electromagnetic radiation from all
emission channels within the LCFS. It excludes radiation emitted in the
scrape-off layer, divertor, and other plasma regions outside the LCFS; it is
therefore distinct from [total plasma radiated
power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power), which integrates radiation over
the full plasma volume.

The integrand is the local [power density due to
radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation), and integration over the
core region gives its corresponding regional total.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_neutral_density_of_isotope_to_difference_of_total_neutral_density_and_neutral_density_of_isotope
NAMES.short:
Odds ratio of the neutral density of a selected hydrogen isotope to the
summed neutral density of all other hydrogen isotopes, distinguishing
composition odds from total isotope fraction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the neutral-population odds ratio for one selected hydrogen
isotope relative to all other hydrogen isotopes. It characterizes isotope
composition using neutral atoms only, with the comparison population
aggregated across every other isotope.

$$
R_i = \frac{n_i}{\sum_{j \ne i} n_j}
$$

Here, $R_i$ is the isotope density ratio, $i$ identifies the selected
hydrogen isotope, $n_i$ is its neutral number density, and $n_j$ is the
neutral number density of another hydrogen isotope. The summation includes
all hydrogen isotopes other than the selected isotope.

The denominator is a total over the other neutral isotope populations, while
the numerator contains only the selected isotope. This quantity excludes
ionized populations and differs from
[total_hydrogenic_density](name:total_hydrogenic_density), which includes
the hydrogenic population across its applicable charge states and isotopes.
It is an odds ratio rather than the selected isotope's fraction of the total
neutral population; if $f_i$ denotes that corresponding neutral isotope
fraction, then $f_i = R_i/(1+R_i)$.

sources.leaf_definition: Ratio of the density of neutrals of this isotope over the summed neutral densities of all other isotopes described in the ../isotope array
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: spectral_bremsstrahlung_photon_radiance
NAMES.short:
Spectrally resolved photon-number radiance of free-free bremsstrahlung,
giving the directional photon emission rate per projected area and
wavelength interval.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the photon-number radiance of the continuum produced by
free-free electron–ion interactions in a plasma. It describes the
directional spectral brightness of bremsstrahlung rather than the emitted
electromagnetic energy.

The spectral photon radiance is defined by

$$
L_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{ff}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^{4}N_{\gamma}}{\mathrm{d}A_{\mathrm{proj}}\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}\Omega\,\mathrm{d}\lambda}
$$

where $L_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{ff}}$ is the free-free spectral photon radiance,
$N_{\gamma}$ is the photon number, $A_{\mathrm{proj}}$ is projected
collecting area normal to the viewing direction, $t$ is time, $\Omega$ is
solid angle, and $\lambda$ is photon wavelength.

The quantity applies to the bremsstrahlung continuum, is differential in
wavelength and viewing solid angle, and counts photons rather than weighting
them by photon energy. It is not integrated over an identified spectral line
and does not represent total bremsstrahlung power.

The broader [spectral photon radiance](name:spectral_photon_radiance)
includes spectral photon emission without restricting the source to
bremsstrahlung, while [photon radiance at a spectral
line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line) represents emission integrated
over a discrete transition interval. Integrating this quantity over a
selected wavelength band gives the corresponding band-integrated photon
radiance, such as [brightness of a visible
camera](name:brightness_of_visible_camera).

NAMES.name: spectral_photon_radiance
NAMES.short:
Calibrated spectral photon radiance of plasma emission, giving photon rate
per projected area, solid angle, and wavelength interval along a viewing
direction.
NAMES.long:
Spectral photon radiance is the photon-number emission rate associated with
a specified viewing direction, projected emitting area, and wavelength
interval. It describes the angular and spectral distribution of plasma
radiation before integration over wavelength or solid angle.

The defining differential relation is

$$
L_\lambda(\lambda,\Omega) = \frac{d^3 N_\gamma}{dA_\perp\,dt\,d\Omega\,d\lambda}
$$

where $L_\lambda$ is the spectral photon radiance, $N_\gamma$ is the number
of emitted photons, $A_\perp$ is the projected emitting area, $t$ is time,
$\Omega$ is solid angle about the viewing direction, and $\lambda$ is photon
wavelength.

This generic quantity includes the photon-number contributions from all
unresolved emitting populations and mechanisms within the specified spectral
and angular element. Its aggregation is differential in wavelength and solid
angle, and it is not restricted to a particular species, reaction, or plasma
region. It is not a volumetric photon-production rate and is not integrated
over a spectral line, wavelength band, or viewing solid angle.

Integrating the spectral radiance over a selected emission-line interval
gives the corresponding [photon radiance at a spectral
line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line). The free-free contribution is
represented by the mechanism-specific [spectral bremsstrahlung rate], while
this quantity includes that contribution only as part of the total emission
when no mechanism qualifier is present.

NAMES.name: spectral_rate_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short:
Detected photoelectron rate assigned to each wavelength pixel of a
spectrometer channel after electronic gain compensation and relative
calibration, but before absolute radiometric calibration.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the spectrally resolved detection rate of photoelectrons
produced by a spectrometer channel. It represents the channel response at an
individual wavelength pixel rather than an absolutely calibrated optical
emission quantity.

The rate for wavelength pixel $p$ is defined by

$$
R_p = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{pe},p}}{dt}
$$

where $R_p$ is the detected photoelectron rate for pixel $p$,
$N_{\mathrm{pe},p}$ is the detected photoelectron count assigned to that
pixel, and $t$ is time.

The quantity applies separately to each wavelength pixel of the spectrometer
channel, with electronic gain compensation and relative channel calibration
applied. It is not summed over the spectral range, and it is not an absolute
radiance or photon-flux measurement.

Summing the rates over pixels that contain an identified spectral feature
produces the corresponding line-integrated signal, represented by [intensity
at spectral line](name:intensity_at_spectral_line). The electrical output
[voltage of spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel) is a
distinct signal quantity and is not this photoelectron rate.

NAMES.name: spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element
NAMES.short:
Photon vacuum wavelength values defining the spectral coordinate for a soft
X-ray filter window’s wavelength-dependent optical response.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vacuum wavelength of photons at which the optical
response of a soft X-ray filter window is specified. It identifies the
spectral position of each response value.

The wavelength–frequency relation is

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the photon vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light
in vacuum, and $\nu$ is the photon frequency.

The quantity applies to the spectral response of the filter window and uses
one wavelength coordinate at a time; it is not a band-integrated response or
a nominal filter-center value. It is distinct from the geometric [thickness
of the filter](name:thickness_of_filter) and from the nominal [wavelength of
the filter](name:wavelength_of_filter).

Wavelength-dependent response quantities, including [spectral absorptivity
of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter) and [spectral
efficiency of the filter](name:spectral_efficiency_of_filter), are functions
evaluated at this wavelength coordinate.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short:
Thermodynamic temperature of the soft X-ray detector assembly, describing
its physical thermal state for calibration and monitoring rather than a
plasma temperature inferred from radiation.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the thermodynamic temperature of the physical soft X-ray
detector assembly and describes the thermal state of its hardware.

It applies to the detector object as a whole, with no implied plasma
population, spatial subcomponent, or charge-state aggregation. It is
distinct from the plasma electron temperature inferred from detected soft
X-ray radiation and does not represent a photon-energy or spectral-response
quantity.

The temperature is the thermal operating state relevant to calibration and
hardware-condition monitoring. It is conceptually analogous to [temperature
of neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector), while [spectral
efficiency of soft X-ray
detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_soft_xray_detector) describes
photon-registration probability rather than detector hardware temperature.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_filter
NAMES.short:
Geometric thickness of one diagnostic filter window, determining the amount
of material available for photon attenuation and spectral selection.
NAMES.long:
Filter thickness is the geometric separation of the two opposing surfaces of
one filter window, measured locally along the material normal. It represents
the material thickness itself rather than a photon path length through the
window.

For corresponding points on the opposing surfaces, the local thickness is
defined by

$$
d = \left| (\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right|
$$

where $d$ is the filter thickness, $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are the
position vectors of the corresponding surface points, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$
is the local unit normal to the filter surface.

This quantity applies to the material of a single filter window used for
X-ray spectral selection, including soft-X-ray, hard-X-ray, and
crystal-spectrometer filter windows. It is not a sum over multiple windows,
diagnostic channels, or detector elements, and it is distinct from the
longer oblique photon path through the material.

For homogeneous material at normal incidence, thickness enters the
attenuation relation $T(E) = \exp[-\mu(E)d]$, where $T(E)$ is photon
transmission at energy $E$, $E$ is photon energy, and $\mu(E)$ is the
material attenuation coefficient. Thus, thickness is a geometric input to
[spectral absorptivity of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter),
whereas [filter width] describes the wavelength span of the transmitted
passband rather than the material dimension.

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_at_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
Azimuthal coordinate locating the geometric center of each detector pixel in
the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate at a detector pixel is the azimuthal angle of that
pixel's geometric center about the machine symmetry axis. It identifies the
center position, not the pixel's orientation, size, or angular extent.

The center position is represented in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame by

$$
\mathbf{r}_{\rm pix}=R_{\rm pix}\hat{\mathbf{R}}(\phi_{\rm pix})+Z_{\rm pix}\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\rm pix}$ is the position vector of the pixel center,
$R_{\rm pix}$ is its major-radius coordinate, $\phi_{\rm pix}$ is its
toroidal coordinate, $Z_{\rm pix}$ is its vertical coordinate, and
$\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ are the radial and vertical unit
vectors. The basis is right-handed, with
$\hat{\mathbf{R}}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}=\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, where
$\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector.

The quantity is defined separately at the geometric center of each detector
pixel; it is not averaged over pixels or assigned to the detector as a
whole. It describes a position coordinate rather than a ray direction, pixel
orientation, or pixel angular width. The [vertical coordinate of the
detector pixel](name:vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel) supplies the
corresponding vertical location, while the [toroidal coordinate of the
detector](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_detector) refers to the detector
center and is not a substitute for this pixel-resolved coordinate.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $\phi_{\rm pix}$ increases in the
$+\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Toroidal coordinate of a camera's geometric center in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where φ is the toroidal angle about the machine
symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal coordinate of a camera is the angular coordinate $\phi_c$ of the
camera's geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame. It specifies the position of that center around the machine symmetry
axis.

The camera center has cylindrical coordinates $(R_c, \phi_c, Z_c)$:

$$
\mathbf{r}_c \leftrightarrow (R_c, \phi_c, Z_c)
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_c$ is the position vector of the camera's geometric
center, $R_c$ is the [radial coordinate of the
camera](name:radial_coordinate_of_camera), and $Z_c$ is the [vertical
coordinate of the camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera).

This quantity locates the camera center only; it is not an orientation
angle, viewing direction, or field-of-view angle of the camera.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the camera center is displaced in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed
from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short:
Toroidal angular coordinate of the first reference point on a diagnostic
line of sight, locating that point around the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate of a line of sight is the azimuthal angle of its
first reference point about the machine symmetry axis. It specifies the
point's circumferential location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame.

For a point expressed in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y},
\hat{z})$ basis, the toroidal angle is defined by

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the first
reference point, and $\phi=0$ is the facility-defined toroidal reference
direction.

This quantity applies specifically to the first reference point of a
diagnostic line of sight. It is a point coordinate, not an angle describing
the line-of-sight direction, and it is not an aggregate over the line or
over multiple reference points. Unlike
[toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element),
which locates an optical-element center, it locates the designated first
line-of-sight point.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the angular displacement from the $\phi=0$
reference direction is counter-clockwise when viewed from above the
$+\hat{Z}$ axis.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_radiated_power
NAMES.short:
Total plasma radiated power is the electromagnetic power emitted by the full
plasma, summed over all photon-emission mechanisms and integrated over the
plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma radiated power is the total rate at which electromagnetic
radiation carries energy away from the plasma. It is the full-plasma
radiation loss quantity formed from all photon-emission mechanisms,
including line radiation, bremsstrahlung, recombination, synchrotron, and
any other radiative emission present.

The defining relation is the volume integral of the local radiation power
density over the plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rad}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is total plasma radiated power,
$V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the full plasma volume,
$p_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the [power density due to
radiation](name:power_density_due_to_radiation) at position $\mathbf{r}$,
and $dV$ is the volume element.

The scope is the plasma as a whole; the aggregation convention is
integration over the full plasma volume together with summation over all
electromagnetic emission mechanisms and spectral contributions. It is not a
region-restricted quantity such as [radiated power over core
region](name:radiated_power_over_core_region), and it is not a
diagnostic-channel signal or line-of-sight quantity.

[Bremsstrahlung power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) is one radiative
contribution when defined for the same plasma population, whereas total
plasma radiated power includes all radiative contributions. [Total neutron
power] is distinct because it is kinetic energy carried by neutrons rather
than electromagnetic radiation. In an energy balance, total plasma radiated
power is a non-negative emitted power that enters as a loss according to the
balance convention; it is not itself a signed source term.

NAMES.name: upper_photon_energy
NAMES.short:
High-energy boundary of an X-ray photon-acceptance band, defining the
maximum photon energy included in a selected spectral window.
NAMES.long:
Upper photon energy is the high-energy edge of an X-ray spectral band used
to select photons or define an energy-resolved emissivity interval. It
identifies a band boundary, not a representative photon energy for the band.

For a band bounded by lower and upper photon energies, the accepted interval
is defined by

$$
E_{\rm lower} \leq E_\gamma \leq E_{\rm upper}
$$

where $E_\gamma$ is the photon energy, $E_{\rm lower}$ is the lower
photon-energy boundary, and $E_{\rm upper}$ is this quantity.

The quantity applies to one selected X-ray spectral band used for channel
counting or for an emissivity quantity. It is one upper boundary for that
band; no summation or averaging over channels, bands, or photon energies is
implied.

Together with the corresponding lower boundary, it fixes the spectral
window. It is distinct from [energy of detector
pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), which denotes a central or
representative energy, while [upper bound energy of detector
pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) applies the same
upper-edge concept specifically to an individual detector pixel.

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short:
Upper wavelength of a filter is the vacuum-wavelength coordinate marking the
long-wavelength, low-frequency edge of its transmitted spectral band.
NAMES.long:
Upper wavelength of a filter is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum
wavelength, that identifies the long-wavelength boundary of a filter's
transmitted spectral band. It is a property of the filter transmission
response, rather than the rest-frame wavelength of a spectral line or the
wavelength inside a material medium.

For the upper boundary associated with the lower temporal frequency, the
vacuum wavelength is defined by:

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\mathrm{low}}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the upper boundary vacuum wavelength,
$c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_{\mathrm{low}}$ is the lower
temporal frequency corresponding to that boundary.

This quantity applies specifically to the long-wavelength boundary of the
transmitted passband and is not a band-average or a full transmission
function. It complements the [lower wavelength of a
filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter), which marks the short-wavelength
boundary; together, the two boundaries determine the [width of a filter].
The parent [wavelength of a filter](name:wavelength_of_filter) also includes
nominal characteristic wavelengths such as a reference wavelength.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical coordinate of the camera's geometric center, measured along
Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the vertical position of the geometric center of a camera
used in a radiation-measurement system. It identifies the camera center as a
physical location in the machine coordinate frame, rather than as a property
of the observed plasma.

The vertical coordinate is the projection of the camera-center position
vector onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
z_{\rm cam} = \mathbf{r}_{\rm cam} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $z_{\rm cam}$ is the camera-center vertical coordinate,
$\mathbf{r}_{\rm cam}$ is the position vector of the camera's geometric
center, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major-radius direction,
$\phi$ the toroidal-angle direction, and $Z$ the vertical direction.

This quantity applies to the camera hardware as a whole and refers
specifically to its geometric center. It is a single positional coordinate,
not a surface average, line-of-sight coordinate, image coordinate, or
coordinate of the plasma region being observed. It must be distinguished
from the analogous aperture location described by [vertical coordinate of an
aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture) and from the vertical
coordinate of a generic measurement location described by [vertical
coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position).

Together with the camera center's radial and toroidal coordinates, this
quantity specifies its location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi,
Z)$ frame. It does not describe the camera's vertical angular coverage,
which is a separate geometric property.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the camera center lies in the direction of
increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
Vertical coordinate locating the geometric center of an individual detector
pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vertical position of the geometric center of one
detector pixel. It locates that center along the cylindrical $Z$ direction
rather than describing a pixel dimension, boundary, or radiation signal.

The coordinate is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height. It applies separately to each detector pixel and is neither
summed nor averaged over pixels, channels, detectors, or cameras.

The quantity describes the center point of the pixel and excludes pixel
span, edge coordinates, detector response, and any detector-local coordinate
components. Together with the [radial coordinate of a detector
pixel](name:radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel), it locates the same pixel
center in the cylindrical $R$-$Z$ plane. Its generic detector-pixel scope
distinguishes it from the corresponding coordinate defined for a
specifically identified [soft X-ray
detector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short:
Characteristic vacuum wavelength assigned to an atomic, ionic, molecular, or
nuclear spectral transition, identifying its central line position.
NAMES.long:
The wavelength of a spectral line is the characteristic vacuum spectral
coordinate of an emission or absorption transition. It identifies the
central line position associated with the transition or processed spectral
feature.

For an unshifted transition, the vacuum wavelength is related to the
transition energy by:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{hc}{\Delta E}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the unshifted vacuum wavelength, $h$ is Planck's
constant, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\Delta E$ is the energy
difference between the transition's quantum states.

The quantity applies to one identified atomic, ionic, molecular, or nuclear
spectral line and is a central wavelength, not a wavelength interval,
spectral width, or aggregate over multiple lines. Depending on the
spectral-line definition, it may denote the unshifted transition reference
or a central wavelength that includes a physical shift of the observed
feature; it is not inherently a wavelength displacement.

This quantity specializes the broader wavelength concept by locating a
spectral transition. A displacement from a specified reference wavelength is
represented separately by
[difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line).

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short:
Translational kinetic temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of the
cold neutral population, based on random translational motion after removal
of its bulk flow.
NAMES.long:
Translational kinetic temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of the
cold neutral population, based on random translational motion after removal
of its bulk flow. It characterizes the low-energy neutral component
associated with a selected hydrogen isotope.

For the cold neutral population, the translational temperature is defined by

$$
T_c = \frac{2}{3 n_c}\int \frac{1}{2}m_c \lvert\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_c\rvert^2 f_c(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

Here $T_c$ is the cold-neutral translational temperature, $n_c$ is the
cold-neutral number density, $m_c$ is the mass of a cold neutral atom,
$\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathbf{u}_c$ is the bulk velocity of
the cold neutral population, $f_c(\mathbf{v})$ is its velocity distribution,
and $d^3v$ is differential volume in velocity space. The distribution is
normalized by $n_c=\int f_c(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v$.

The quantity applies to the low-energy neutral-atom population in the plasma
edge or scrape-off layer and is specific to the selected hydrogen isotope.
It is averaged over particles in that cold population, not summed with the
energetic neutral population or with other isotopes. It excludes bulk flow
energy and does not represent a temperature associated with an internal
quantum or excitation state.

This quantity is the cold-population specialization of [neutral
temperature](name:neutral_temperature), while [hot neutral
temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature) applies the same translational
definition to the energetic neutral population. Unlike [volume-averaged
neutral temperature](name:volume_averaged_neutral_temperature), it is not
defined by averaging the temperature over a plasma volume.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short:
Major-radius location of a camera’s geometric center, measured from the
toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a camera is the major-radius position of its
geometric center, measured perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. It
identifies the camera center rather than any individual detector pixel,
aperture, or line-of-sight point.

The coordinate is defined from the Cartesian coordinates of the camera
center:

$$
R_{\mathrm{cam}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{cam}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{cam}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{cam}}$ is the camera-center radial coordinate, and
$x_{\mathrm{cam}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{cam}}$ are the camera-center coordinates
in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis. The
corresponding cylindrical frame is the right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height.

This quantity applies to the geometric center of the camera as a whole and
is not an average over pixels, viewing directions, or detector elements. It
is the camera-specific specialization of the parent [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). Together with the [vertical coordinate
of the camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera) and [toroidal coordinate
of the camera](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_camera), it specifies the
camera-center position.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a detector pixel’s geometric center, locating the
pixel relative to the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center of an
individual detector pixel. It identifies the pixel center’s perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Using the corresponding right-handed Cartesian basis $(x, y, z)$, with the
symmetry axis at $x=y=0$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{pix}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{pix}}^2+y_{\mathrm{pix}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{pix}}$ is the pixel-center major-radius coordinate, and
$x_{\mathrm{pix}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{pix}}$ are the Cartesian coordinates of
that center perpendicular to the symmetry axis.

The quantity applies to each detector-pixel center individually; it is not
an average over pixels, a radiation-weighted position, or the radial
coordinate of the camera as a whole. It is the detector-pixel specialization
of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), while the corresponding
vertical location is given by the [vertical coordinate of detector
pixel](name:vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short:
Major-radius coordinate of a specified geometric point associated with a
line of sight, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of a specified geometric point
associated with a line of sight. It locates that point by its perpendicular
distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical
$(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
R_{\mathrm{los}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{los}}^2+y_{\mathrm{los}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{los}}$ is the radial coordinate of the specified
line-of-sight point, and $x_{\mathrm{los}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{los}}$ are the
horizontal Cartesian coordinate values of that point in the right-handed
Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, whose origin lies on the
toroidal symmetry axis.

The quantity is geometric and pointwise: it applies to a designated point
associated with a line of sight and has no plasma-population or regional
aggregation. A line of sight can contain multiple such points, so this name
alone does not select a first point, second point, third point, endpoint,
line-integrated radius, or averaged radius.

It is a locus-specific instance of the general [radial
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) quantity, with the line of sight
identifying the associated geometric locus rather than defining a new
radial-coordinate concept.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angular_width_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Full toroidal angular span of one limiter tile between its minimum and
maximum φ coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angular width of an individual limiter tile is the full angular
span occupied by that tile around the machine symmetry axis. It is a
non-negative geometric extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is
vertical height.

The width is defined from the extrema of the tile's toroidal-angle extent:

$$
\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}} = \phi_{\max} - \phi_{\min}
$$

where $\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the tile's toroidal angular width, and
$\phi_{\max}$ and $\phi_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum toroidal-angle
coordinates of the tile, evaluated on a continuous angular branch when the
extent crosses the angular periodic boundary.

This quantity applies to one individual limiter tile and represents its
complete toroidal span; it is not summed over tiles, limiter units, or
periodic repetitions. It is distinct from a toroidal-angle coordinate, a
tile-center angle, and the angular width of an entire limiter assembly.

The toroidal extent complements the boundary geometry described by the
[vertical outline of the limiter
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile), while the analogous camera
field-of-view quantity [toroidal angular width of a
camera](name:toroidal_angular_width_of_camera) applies to an optical viewing
extent rather than a structural tile.

sources.leaf_definition: Simplified description of toroidal angle extensions of the unit, by a list of zones defined by their centre and full width (in toroidal angle).  In each of these zones, the unit outline remains the same. Leave this node empty for an axisymmetric unit. The first dimension gives the centre and full width toroidal angle values for the unit. The second dimension represents the toroidal occurrences of the unit countour (i.e. the number of toroidal zones).
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units. Whenever relevant, multiple units should be ordered so that they define contiguous sections, clockwise in the poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short:
Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of each point on a limiter-tile boundary
contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline of a limiter tile gives the signed vertical coordinate
of each point on the tile’s geometric boundary contour. It describes the
contour geometry rather than a material property, thickness, or surface-load
quantity.

For contour point $i$, the vertical coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is its
position vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here, $R$ is major radius,
$\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies pointwise to the irregular outline of one limiter tile
in its poloidal cross section. The contour is closed by connecting its final
point to its initial point, without duplicating the initial point; no
averaging, summation, or other aggregation over contour points is implied.
Unlike the [radial outline of a limiter
tile](name:radial_outline_of_limiter_tile), this quantity gives the vertical
coordinate rather than the major-radius coordinate of the boundary.

The same geometric carrier and coordinate meaning apply to the [vertical
outline of a divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but
that related quantity belongs to a divertor tile rather than a limiter tile.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the contour point lies toward increasing $Z$
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short:
The vertical coordinate of each point on a plasma-facing component boundary
outline is the signed height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height $Z$ of each
boundary-contour point belonging to a plasma-facing component. It describes
the component boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For outline point $i$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is that
point's position vector relative to the cylindrical coordinate origin, and
$\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unit vector in the vertical direction. The
quantity applies pointwise to one component boundary outline and is not an
average, extremum, centroid coordinate, or integrated geometric measure. A
closed outline does not repeat its first point as a closing point.

This coordinate has the same geometric meaning as the corresponding outline
coordinate for a limiter tile or divertor tile, such as [vertical outline of
limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile) and [vertical outline
of divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but its locus is
the plasma-facing component boundary in general.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when $Z_i$ increases in the $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$
direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the mobile unit, for a set of time slices. Repeat the first point in case of a closed contour

NAMES.name: atomic_count
NAMES.short:
Stoichiometric multiplicity of a selected element within the chemical
formula of an atomic or molecular species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the number of atoms belonging to a selected element in one
atomic or molecular species, as specified by its composition. It is a
composition property rather than a particle population or field quantity.

For an atomic species, the count is one for its constituent element; for a
molecular species, it is the element's stoichiometric coefficient in the
molecular formula. The count applies to the selected species composition and
is not a number density, abundance, or present/absent flag. It is not summed
over particles or charge states, and changing the ionization state does not
change the elemental atom count.

The selected element is identified independently by its [atomic
number](name:atomic_number), while this quantity gives the number of atoms
of that element in the species. The same composition count can therefore be
used for neutral or ionized forms of a species and for elemental
constituents of reaction participants.

NAMES.name: atomic_mass
NAMES.short:
Mass parameter assigned to a specified ion or neutral particle species,
encoding its isotope or constituent composition for inertial and transport
calculations.
NAMES.long:
Atomic mass is the intrinsic mass parameter assigned to one specified ion or
neutral particle species. It identifies an isotope for an atomic species or
the constituent composition for a molecular or compound neutral, and
provides the inertial scale used in collisional and transport physics.

The mass is represented relative to the atomic mass unit by

$$
m_s = A_s m_u
$$

where $m_s$ is the atomic mass of the specified species, $A_s$ is its
relative atomic mass, and $m_u$ is the atomic mass unit.

The scope is one species definition at a time: either an ion species or a
neutral particle species. No aggregation over separate species, charge
states, or plasma populations is implied; for a molecular or compound
neutral, combining constituent masses is part of that species definition.
The ion-specific form [ion atomic mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) and
neutral-specific form [neutral species atomic
mass](name:neutral_species_atomic_mass) are corresponding instances of this
quantity.

Atomic masses provide the species-dependent weighting used when forming
aggregate quantities such as [total plasma mass
density](name:total_plasma_mass_density); they are not themselves densities,
particle counts, or aggregate plasma masses.

NAMES.name: atomic_number
NAMES.short:
Nuclear proton count identifying the selected element in a plasma or
neutral-particle species, independent of isotope and ionization state.
NAMES.long:
Atomic number identifies an element through the number of protons in its
nucleus. It is an intrinsic element identifier that remains unchanged when
the element is bound in a molecule or changes ionization state.

The atomic number $Z$ is defined by

$$
Z = N_p
$$

where $N_p$ is the number of protons in the element's nucleus.

This quantity applies to the selected element constituent of a neutral or
charged species, including an element within a compound or molecule. It
identifies one element and is not summed over constituent elements,
isotopes, or charge states.

Atomic number is distinct from [ion charge](name:ion_charge), which
describes the net electric charge of an ion and may change while $Z$ remains
fixed. Unlike [fast ion atomic number](name:fast_ion_atomic_number), this
generic identifier carries no fixed fast-ion role or diagnostic context.

NAMES.name: difference_of_total_plasma_heating_power_and_time_derivative_of_plasma_stored_energy
NAMES.short:
Instantaneous plasma power available for confinement losses after correcting
total coupled heating for the rate of change of stored plasma energy.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the instantaneous global power-balance residual available
to account for energy leaving the plasma confinement system. It corrects the
total plasma heating power for transient changes in the plasma’s stored
energy.

It is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{loss}} = P_{\mathrm{heat,total}} - \frac{dW_{\mathrm{plasma}}}{dt}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the power-balance residual represented by this
quantity, $P_{\mathrm{heat,total}}$ is the [total plasma heating power],
$W_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the total stored energy of the plasma, and $t$ is
time.

The quantity is global and aggregated over all heating contributions
included in total plasma heating power and over the complete stored
plasma-energy reservoir. It is not the heating input itself, a single-source
heating contribution, or a regional radiation measurement; [radiated power
over the core region](name:radiated_power_over_core_region) is a specific
loss channel rather than this balance residual. A positive value means
heating exceeds the instantaneous increase in stored energy, while a
negative value means stored energy is increasing faster than the heating
input.

This residual is the loss-power term in the conventional energy-confinement
relation $\tau_E = W_{\mathrm{plasma}}/P_{\mathrm{loss}}$, where $\tau_E$ is
the energy confinement time; transient storage changes are therefore
excluded from the inferred loss power rather than counted as losses.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Total power coupled to the plasma minus dW/dt (correcting from transient energy content)

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic
axis is the local electron count per physical volume at that location.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic
axis is the local electron count per physical volume at that location. It
represents electrons specifically, rather than ions, neutrals, or another
plasma population.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_e}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the electron number density at the magnetic
axis, $N_e$ is the number of electrons, and $V$ is physical volume.

The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested
closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient
vanishes. It applies to the complete electron population at that location
and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor an ion or neutral
density.

This is the electron-specific realization of the population-independent
[density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It must be
distinguished from [total ion density at the magnetic
axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts ions, and from
[electron temperature at the magnetic
axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which characterizes
electron energy rather than particle count.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Thermal energy per particle of the electron population, expressed as an
energy-equivalent temperature and evaluated at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
Thermal energy per particle of the electron population, expressed as an
energy-equivalent temperature and evaluated at the magnetic axis. The
magnetic axis is the degenerate innermost magnetic surface of the
equilibrium, where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes;
evaluation at this locus does not imply that the electron temperature has an
extremum there.

For a thermal electron population with a well-defined absolute thermodynamic
temperature, the energy-equivalent electron temperature is defined by:

$$
T_e = k_\mathrm{B}\,\Theta_e
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature expressed as energy per particle,
$\Theta_e$ is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the electrons, and
$k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant.

This quantity applies specifically to the electron population at the
magnetic axis and is an intensive, per-particle quantity rather than a
charge-state sum, volume average, or volume-integrated electron energy. It
excludes ion temperatures, radiative temperature-equivalent scales, and the
total thermal energy content of the electron population.

It is the electron-specific member of the broader [temperature at the
magnetic axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which also encompasses
other populations and radiative temperature interpretations. The
corresponding electron temperature at another locus is [electron temperature
at the outboard midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_outboard_midplane),
while [thermal electron energy](name:thermal_electron_energy) denotes an
integrated energy content rather than this local temperature.

NAMES.name: energy_confinement_time
NAMES.short:
Characteristic timescale for loss of confined plasma thermal energy, defined
as stored thermal energy divided by the net power leaving that energy
reservoir.
NAMES.long:
Energy confinement time is the characteristic timescale on which the
confined plasma loses its stored thermal energy through net outward energy
transport and other thermal-energy loss channels. The stored energy is the
volume-integrated quantity defined by [thermal plasma
energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), not a particle confinement time or the
duration of plasma confinement.

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W_{\mathrm{th}}}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the energy confinement time, $W_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the
stored thermal energy in J, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net power loss
from that thermal-energy reservoir in W. In a stationary power balance,
$P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ equals the net heating power deposited in the plasma. It
is distinct from [plasma confinement time], which denotes the elapsed
duration of confinement rather than an energy-loss timescale.

NAMES.name: loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short:
Toroidal electromotive force evaluated on the last closed flux surface that
drives the conventionally signed ohmic plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The loop voltage at the plasma boundary is the toroidal electromotive force
associated with the inductive electric field around the last closed
magnetic-flux surface. It is the net voltage available to drive the ohmic
component of the confined plasma current.

For a closed toroidal contour $C$ on the last closed flux surface, the loop
voltage is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{loop}} = \oint_C \mathbf{E} \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the loop voltage, $\mathbf{E}$ is the
electric-field vector, $d\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is the directed line element,
and $C$ is oriented in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. The
quantity is a contour-integrated scalar evaluated at the plasma boundary,
not a local electric-field component or an external-coil terminal voltage.

This boundary quantity represents the total loop voltage driving plasma
current, including the inductive contribution associated with changing
poloidal magnetic flux. It excludes no plasma-current-driving contribution
merely because it is externally generated; the narrower [external loop
voltage](name:external_loop_voltage) denotes only the externally generated
contribution and is therefore not equivalent to the total boundary loop
voltage.

The loop voltage is related to the ohmic plasma-current drive through the
toroidal component of the electric field and the plasma conductivity. The
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame uses $R$ for major radius,
$\phi$ for toroidal angle, and $Z$ for vertical height.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the electromotive force drives conventional
plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$,
counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: safety_factor
NAMES.short:
Signed ratio of toroidal to poloidal field-line winding on a magnetic flux
surface, equal to the toroidal turns made during one poloidal circuit.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor $q$ is the signed field-line winding ratio on a magnetic
flux surface. It gives the toroidal winding associated with one poloidal
circuit and is a property of the magnetic equilibrium; when derived from an
equilibrium, it is the value calculated from the reconstructed
magnetic-field geometry.

The defining differential relation is:

$$
q = \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}}
$$

Here, $q$ is the safety factor, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal
magnetic flux associated with the flux surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the
poloidal magnetic flux associated with the flux surface, and $d$ denotes an
infinitesimal differential between neighboring surfaces.

The quantity applies to the magnetic field on each relevant closed or
limiting flux surface in the plasma, without restriction to a species, axis,
or transport channel. This general form represents one value for a selected
flux surface and is neither summed nor averaged over surfaces.

It is distinct from a locus-specific evaluation or an extremum selected over
multiple surfaces. For example, [safety factor at magnetic
axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and [safety factor at plasma
boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary) are evaluations of this
quantity at specified surfaces, whereas [minimum safety
factor](name:minimum_safety_factor) applies an additional minimum-selection
criterion.

The [rotational transform](name:rotational_transform) describes the
reciprocal field-line winding convention, counting poloidal turns per
toroidal circuit rather than toroidal turns per poloidal circuit. Rational
safety-factor values identify surfaces on which field-line winding can close
after a finite number of toroidal and poloidal turns.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when a magnetic field line advances in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ during the positive poloidal
circuit, with orientations defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Isotropic kinetic pressure produced by random motion of bulk thermal
electrons, evaluated in the plasma state immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron pressure is the isotropic scalar stress contribution
produced by random motion of the bulk electron population in the designated
post-sawtooth-crash plasma state. It represents the thermal electron
contribution rather than the pressure of the full electron population.

For an isotropic thermal population, the pressure is defined by

$$
p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = \frac{2}{3} n_{e,\mathrm{th}}\langle E_{e,\mathrm{rand}}\rangle
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron pressure,
$n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the number density of thermal electrons, and $\langle
E_{e,\mathrm{rand}}\rangle$ is their mean random kinetic energy; the
subscripts $e$ and $\mathrm{th}$ identify electrons and the thermal
population, respectively.

The quantity applies only to bulk thermal electrons and is evaluated in the
plasma state immediately following a sawtooth crash. It is an isotropic
scalar contribution, aggregated over the included thermal electrons, and
excludes fast or otherwise nonthermal electron contributions.

It is the thermal component of [total electron
pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), which combines thermal and
suprathermal electron contributions. A fast-particle pressure quantity such
as [fast particle pressure](name:fast_particle_pressure) represents a
distinct nonthermal population and must not be included in this thermal
contribution.

NAMES.name: total_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Kinetic pressure associated with the entire electron population, combining
thermal and suprathermal contributions in the isotropic electron stress.
NAMES.long:
Total electron pressure is the isotropic kinetic part of the electron
pressure tensor, representing random electron momentum transport for the
complete electron population.

For the combined electron distribution function, its defining relation is

$$
p_e = \frac{m_e}{3} \int |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_e|^2 f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_e$ is total electron pressure, $m_e$ is electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$
is electron velocity, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is mean electron velocity, and
$f_e(\mathbf{v})$ is the combined electron velocity distribution function
normalized so its velocity integral gives the electron number density.

The aggregation includes both bulk thermal and suprathermal electrons and
applies across core, edge, and scrape-off-layer plasma. It excludes
anisotropic stress components and is not restricted to the thermal electron
population alone.

This quantity makes the total aggregation explicit within [electron
pressure](name:electron_pressure): it is the sum of the thermal contribution
and the [fast electron pressure](name:fast_electron_pressure) contribution.
The parent name denotes the same isotropic pressure concept without
requiring the total qualifier.
NAMES.sign:
Positive when the isotropic electron stress is compressive
rather than tensile.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_line_averaged_electron_density_to_greenwald_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless Greenwald fraction comparing the electron number density
averaged along a plasma chord with the empirical density limit set by plasma
current and effective minor radius.
NAMES.long:
The Greenwald fraction measures the proximity of a confined plasma's
line-averaged electron density to its empirical Greenwald density limit.

It is defined by:

$$
f_G = \frac{\bar{n}_e}{n_G}
$$

where $f_G$ is the Greenwald fraction, $\bar{n}_e$ is the [line-averaged
electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density), and $n_G$ is the
[Greenwald density](name:greenwald_density) determined from the
plasma-current magnitude and effective minor radius.

The numerator represents the electron population averaged along a plasma
chord; the denominator is the empirical density reference for the confined
plasma. This quantity is a global normalized ratio, not a local electron
density, a density limit itself, or an average over charge states or spatial
regions.

The fraction is the direct normalization of line-averaged electron density
by Greenwald density: values near unity indicate proximity to the empirical
reference limit, while values above or below unity indicate a line-averaged
density respectively above or below that reference.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_line_averaged_hydrogen_density_to_line_averaged_total_hydrogenic_density
NAMES.short:
Dimensionless line-averaged protium fraction among hydrogenic ions, obtained
by dividing the protium density by the total hydrogenic density along the
same chord.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the fraction of hydrogenic ion content carried by protium
along a specified chord through the plasma. It is a ratio of consistently
line-averaged densities, rather than a local fraction or a volume-averaged
fraction.

$$
f_{\rm H}^{\rm line} = \frac{\bar{n}_{\rm H}^{\rm line}}{\bar{n}_{\rm H}^{\rm line}+\bar{n}_{\rm D}^{\rm line}+\bar{n}_{\rm T}^{\rm line}}
$$

where $f_{\rm H}^{\rm line}$ is the line-averaged protium fraction,
$\bar{n}_{\rm H}^{\rm line}$ is the line-averaged protium-ion number
density, $\bar{n}_{\rm D}^{\rm line}$ is the corresponding deuterium-ion
number density, and $\bar{n}_{\rm T}^{\rm line}$ is the corresponding
tritium-ion number density. The symbols H, D, and T denote protium,
deuterium, and tritium, respectively.

The quantity applies to the hydrogenic ion population along one common chord
and aggregates the isotope densities through the total hydrogenic
denominator. Neutral atomic hydrogen and non-hydrogenic species are
excluded. The numerator is the [line-averaged hydrogen
density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density), while the denominator is the
[total hydrogenic density](name:total_hydrogenic_density) under the same
line-averaging convention.

This ratio differs from the [ratio of volume-averaged hydrogen density to
volume-averaged total hydrogenic
density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_hydrogen_density_to_volume_averaged_total_hydrogenic_density),
because the latter uses volume-averaged rather than chord-averaged isotope
densities.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume for the local thermal
electron population, excluding fast and suprathermal electron contributions.
NAMES.long:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume for the local thermal
electron population is the local continuum count density of electrons not
bound to atoms, molecules, or ions that belong to the bulk Maxwellian
electron component.

For the thermal electron distribution, the defining relation is:

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int f_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local thermal electron number
density, $f_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})$ is the thermal-electron
velocity distribution, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron
velocity, and $d^3\mathbf{v}$ is the volume element in velocity space.

This quantity applies only to the local bulk thermal electron population.
Fast and suprathermal electrons are excluded, and the quantity is neither a
chord average nor a volume average. The parent [electron
density](name:electron_density) denotes the unqualified local free-electron
density without this population restriction.

The complete local [total electron density](name:total_electron_density) is
the sum of this thermal component and the corresponding [fast electron
density](name:fast_electron_density) when those components are resolved
separately.

NAMES.name: total_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume for the complete local
population, combining thermal and fast electrons rather than selecting one
population component.
NAMES.long:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume for the complete local
electron population is the local continuum count density of electrons not
bound to atoms, molecules, or ions, including both thermal and fast
nonthermal contributions.

The complete local electron density is defined by:

$$
n_e^{\mathrm{total}} = n_e^{\mathrm{thermal}} + n_e^{\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_e^{\mathrm{total}}$ is the complete local free-electron number
density, $n_e^{\mathrm{thermal}}$ is the density of the local thermal
electron population represented by [thermal electron
density](name:thermal_electron_density), and $n_e^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the
density of the local fast, nonthermal electron population represented by
[fast electron density](name:fast_electron_density).

This quantity applies locally to the full free-electron population and is
aggregated over its thermal and fast components. It excludes electrons bound
in atoms, molecules, or ions, and it is not restricted to either population
component. It is also distinct from [line-averaged electron
density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) and [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), which apply spatial
averaging rather than a local evaluation.

As the complete-population form of [electron
density](name:electron_density), it includes both thermal and nonthermal
contributions. Integrating this local quantity over a specified plasma
volume gives [volume-integrated total electron density], whereas the
component names retain only one electron population.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume averaged over the
plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, giving the global
mean free-electron density.
NAMES.long:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume averaged over the
plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface is the global mean of
the unqualified free-electron density.

For local [electron density](name:electron_density) $n_e(\mathbf{x})$, the
defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_e\rangle_{\rm LCFS} = \frac{1}{V_{\rm LCFS}}\int_{V_{\rm LCFS}} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $\langle n_e\rangle_{\rm LCFS}$ is the volume-averaged electron
density, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local free-electron number density at
spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $V_{\rm LCFS}$ is the plasma volume enclosed
by the last closed flux surface, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a differential volume
element.

The average includes the complete unqualified free-electron population
within the last-closed-flux-surface volume and is not restricted to thermal
or fast electrons. It is a global volume mean rather than a local value and
excludes plasma volume outside that boundary; unlike [line-averaged electron
density](name:line_averaged_electron_density), it is not averaged along a
chord.

This quantity is the volume-averaging transformation of [electron
density](name:electron_density). It provides the common denominator for
volume-averaged elemental abundance ratios, such as the [volume-averaged
argon-to-electron density
ratio](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_argon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density),
whose numerator and denominator are averaged over the same plasma volume.
